articles.title: Ukraine kept this strike drone secret for two years—its maker says it has destroyed more than 350 Russian systems
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone maker has revealed it built a strike weapon it kept classified, deputy director Andrii Rymaruk told Radio NV. For two years, Ukrspecsystems, known for manufacturing Ukraine's SHARK reconnaissance drones, hid its connection to the RAM-2X strike drone, even as crews used it to hunt Russia's costly air defenses and missile launchers deep behind the front. By 2025, it had quietly become the Defense Forces' flagship mid-strike drone.
Ukraine's war on Russia's air defenses increasingly runs on drones its own industry builds and fields in secret, revealed only once they have already destroyed the enemy's costliest launchers and radars. Holding one back that long lets its crews rack up strikes before Moscow can study the weapon and build a counter—and this maker went public only once wrecked drones had reached Russian hands.
Why come out now
The RAM-2X first flew in combat in early 2024, but the maker kept its role secret. Rymaruk said the company wanted the drone and its crews to finish the job first—destroy what needed destroying—before talking. Once shot-down units reached the enemy and turned up on social media, silence no longer protected anything. So after two years, Ukrspecsystems unveiled the drone at the MSPO defense expo in Kielce, Poland.
What it kills
This is a mid-strike drone—a loitering munition that flies deep behind the lines, circles, and dives into its target. Its victims include S-400 and S-300 air defenses, the systems Russia uses to shoot down aircraft, and Iskander launchers that fire ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities.
Rymaruk put the RAM-2X's own tally at more than 350 Russian systems destroyed since 2024, while Defender Media, which interviewed him, reported more than 1,000 targets over two years. Ukrspecsystems credits the wider RAM series, which reaches back to a fixed-wing model supplied from late 2022, with more than 450 target engagements, over 400 of them against air defenses. Today, it destroys 50 to 60 pieces of Russian equipment a month.
How far, how many
The drone has grown fast. It flew 140 km in 2024 and now hits targets up to 180 km, almost 230 km in good conditions, and a crew from the 429th Achilles unmanned-systems brigade set a range record at 215.5 km. It has spread from a few crews to about 100 military units and 250 trained teams, and one operator can fly it from anywhere in Ukraine. It also works in pairs with the SHARK-M reconnaissance drone—one finds the target, the other kills it. In July, Ukrainians crowdfunded 30 of the drones for military intelligence and the security service through Serhii Prytula's foundation.

articles.title: EU pledges €3.3 billion for Ukraine, von der Leyen says “more is coming” as Russia’s escalating air war makes life in Ukrainian cities increasingly difficult
articles.body:
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen says Europe will provide Ukraine with another €3.3 billion for missiles and drones as Russia intensifies attacks on Kyiv and seeks to make daily life in Ukraine's cities impossible.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to its partners for more air defense as Russia develops increasingly sophisticated ways to attack Ukrainian cities, while Ukraine’s stocks of air-defense interceptors have fallen to critically low levels.
Following a call with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, von der Leyen said the EU would disburse the funds on 18 September. She also said the EU had approved funding for Patriot air defense systems through its Ukraine Support Loan.
Ukraine needs more air defense
Russia has increasingly combined large numbers of attack drones with ballistic and cruise missiles, forcing Ukraine to defend vast areas while facing shortages of high-end interceptors.
The most difficult targets are Russia’s ballistic missiles, which can reach Ukrainian cities within minutes and require specialized systems such as Patriot to intercept. Ukraine has repeatedly called for more Patriot batteries and interceptors as Russia increases missile attacks.
Ukraine also needs additional air defense capabilities to counter Russia’s increasingly sophisticated drone attacks. Russia is deploying faster, more advanced Geran-type drones that are more difficult to intercept, increasing pressure on Ukraine’s already limited air-defense stocks.
Von der Leyen said the EU had approved funding for Patriot systems last week, but acknowledged that “clearly more is needed.”
The new €3.3 billion package will fund the procurement of missiles and drones for Ukraine, strengthening its ability to defend against Russian attacks.
Europe proposes joint air defense development
Von der Leyen also announced that the EU is prepared to use remaining funds from its Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program to launch a new joint EU-Ukraine defense initiative.
The proposed program would focus on developing a European air and missile defense system, building on the jointly developed anti-ballistic Freya system.
The goal is to combine Ukraine’s battlefield experience and defense innovation with European technology and industrial capacity, according to von der Leyen.
The announcement comes as Ukraine is trying to strengthen its air defenses ahead of another winter of Russian attacks, when strikes against energy and other critical infrastructure could have an especially severe impact on civilians.
The EU has billions in unspent defense funds. It wants to use them for projects with Ukraine
Von der Leyen calls for broader support
Von der Leyen said the EU has already mobilized nearly €15 billion for Ukraine in 2026, with additional support planned. She added that “more is coming.”
She also said Ukraine needs to complete reforms in the Verkhovna Rada to unlock further funding and continue its path toward EU membership.
“Europe is stepping up,” von der Leyen said. “Now others must step up their support too.”

articles.title: Russia employs thousands of North Koreans to build combat drones, sanctions monitors say
articles.body:
Russia is increasingly using North Korean citizens to assemble combat drones for its war against Ukraine, circumventing international sanctions while providing Pyongyang with an important source of foreign currency, according to a report published by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) on Sept. 16. Over the past year, North Korean migrant workers abroad generated as much as $800 million for Kim Jong Un’s government, which used the funds to finance nuclear and missile programs in violation of UN Security Council resolutions, the report states.
The report estimates that as many as 25,000 North Koreans are employed in Russia’s drone industry, including at facilities in the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan, where Geran-type attack drones, modeled on Iran’s Shahed series, are assembled. Russia gains a new pool of workers for industries supporting its war against Ukraine while further eroding a sanctions regime against Pyongyang that Moscow itself once helped enforce.
According to the MSMT, North Korean workers in Russia are often categorized as students under a special visa arrangement that allows sanctions to be circumvented without the need for a formal breach. One “student” worker earns an average of about $7,500 a year, the report said, with most of that money confiscated by the North Korean government.
Monthly pay in Russia can be up to five times higher than in China, making Russia an increasingly attractive destination for Pyongyang to send such laborers. Still, as of the end of 2025, between 20,000 and 70,000 North Koreans were working in China, compared with 15,000 to 30,000 in Russia.
“DPRKauthorities also exercise extreme control over labourers’ movement and interactions with outsiders in order to prevent defections, while labourers who do defect risk reprisals against family members remaining in North Korea,” the report said.
It was previously reported that North Korean workers at construction sites in three Russian cities were working up to 16 hours a day with virtually no days off and receiving no more than $10 a month after deductions. Their passports were confiscated by representatives of North Korean security services, and the workers often did not know who their actual employer was because Russian companies hired them in violation of UN sanctions.
The MSMT, which includes the United States, South Korea, Japan and eight other countries, was established in 2024 after Russia blocked the renewal of the mandate for a UN panel that had monitored compliance with sanctions against Pyongyang for 15 years.

articles.title: The US House just passed the first major Russia oil sanctions in two years—one signature stands between them and law
articles.body:
The US House of Representatives has approved sweeping new sanctions on Russia and the countries and companies that help finance its war, sending the measure to the president to sign into law, The Hill reported. The vote breaks a nearly two-year stretch in which Congress passed no major measure to back Ukraine. It also hands Washington fresh power to choke the oil money that keeps Moscow's war running.
For most of the full-scale war, US backing for Kyiv came through emergency spending battles, not laws built to cut off Moscow's income. Washington's long wager that negotiations would end the fighting kept its sharpest economic tools on the shelf. That bet has now shifted toward squeezing the customers who keep the Kremlin's oil trade alive.
The vote and what comes next
In the House, 58 Democrats broke from their party's leaders on 16 September to join most Republicans. The bill passed 262-159, with 203 Republicans and one independent also voting yes, and seven Republicans joining 152 Democrats against.
Whether the full weight of the bill lands is now Trump's call. A White House official said he planned to sign it, and the White House had pushed House Republican leaders to move it. The bill directs him to impose the tariffs and mandates sanctions on Putin, senior officials, and Russian banks, though he can waive them by certifying that it serves US national interests, and how far he goes stays uncertain.
His posture on Russia keeps shifting. Days before the vote, he urged Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries. He said the strikes were pushing diesel prices up worldwide. Those same strikes drain the war economy this bill sets out to squeeze.
What the sanctions do
The bill directs Washington to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five biggest buyers of Russian crude, the five biggest buyers of its gas, and the five countries doing most to help Moscow evade oil sanctions—a target aimed squarely at China and India. Countries whose Russian gas imports are less than 15% of everything Russia exports in gas, and that take significant steps to cut them, would be exempt from the gas-based tariff. There is no such carve-out for crude.
It also blacklists Russian officials, banks, and the aging tankers of Russia's shadow fleet, the vessels that move sanctioned crude around Western restrictions. The measure also extends US sanctions on Iran's energy and weapons sectors, a piece Trump asked for. That is why the bill's full name is the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.
US sanctions 13 Iran-Belarus-China entities supplying Iran’s IRGC. That’s three of four “Axis of Upheaval” states
Why a stalled bill finally moved
For more than a year, the package sat frozen. It had a veto-proof majority of co-sponsors, but the White House wanted room to negotiate with Moscow, and the bill never reached a vote. Its author, Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, spent more than a year negotiating the measure before he died in July. Lawmakers in both parties revived and fast-tracked it in his name, and Trump dropped his resistance and signaled he would sign.
Not everyone wanted it. Most House Democrats voted against, saying the bill hands the president broad new tariff powers and lets him waive away the sanctions it claims to impose. Nearly a dozen Republicans privately pressed leaders to strip the new powers out, alarmed they could push up prices at home before the midterm elections. Their leaders moved it through anyway. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had lobbied for weeks, even watching an early Senate vote from the chamber.
"To Vladimir Putin—we have your number," said Senator Richard Blumenthal, who co-wrote the bill, after the vote. "And to Ukraine—you are not alone."
Kyiv's response
Ukraine welcomed the vote within hours. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha thanked the House for its bipartisan leadership and said Ukraine honors Graham's legacy. Parliament speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk thanked both chambers of Congress and House Speaker Mike Johnson. He singled out Blumenthal for carrying the bill through after Graham's death. What matters for Ukraine, Stefanchuk said, is that pressure on Russia's war funding is turning into concrete decisions.
President Zelenskyy called the timing symbolic: the House voted during another Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine. The bill and other strong sanctions steps are "an extremely powerful instrument capable of stopping this terrorist war," he said.

articles.title: Fresh Russian Strikes Hit Ukraine As US House Passes Sanctions Bill Targeting Moscow
articles.body:
Russia resumed its missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities on September 17, hours after the US Congress passed a sanctions package that supporters say will increase pressure on Moscow and countries that help it finance its war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was "symbolic" that the US House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 amid another Russian ballistic missile and drone attack on Ukraine.
He said Russian strikes hit civilian and energy infrastructure in eight regions, damaging homes in the capital, Kyiv, and the major southern port city of Odesa and injuring dozens of people, including children.
"The Lindsey Graham bill, along with other strong sanctions steps by our partners against the source of this war -- against Russia -- is an extremely powerful tool that can stop this terrorist war and bring Russia to the point where it has to make peace," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha welcomed the passage of the Russia sanctions bill, calling it a strong response to Moscow's continued attacks on Ukraine.
However, he also urged further sanctions, including a full embargo, restrictions on Russia's so-called shadow fleet, and blocking sanctions targeting its military-industrial complex.
"We can stop Putin by depriving him of the resources to continue this war," Sybiha wrote on X.
Following the latest Russian attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 18 people, including children, had been injured in the city, while a repeat drone strike sparked a fire in an administrative building.
In Odesa, regional authorities said a Russian overnight strike injured six people, including two children, and damaged residential buildings, a private home, and infrastructure.
Zaporizhzhya, in southeastern Ukraine, was also hit by a Russian missile strike that injured three people and damaged industrial facilities, according to regional authorities.
Later in the day, regional Governor Mykhaylo Semikin said at least five more people were injured when a Russian first-person-view (FPV) drone hit a bus carrying civilians.
Meanwhile, Russian officials reported that a Ukrainian drone attack damaged an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl.
Authorities in Russia's Krasnodar region said drone debris sparked a fire at an oil refinery, which was quickly extinguished. No injuries reported.
The refinery, located about 250 kilometers northeast of Moscow, had previously been targeted by Ukrainian drones and halted processing at two of its three crude distillation units following the August attack.
Zelenskyy confirmed the attack on the Yaroslavl oil refinery, adding that Ukraine's Security Service had carried out a strike on a military airfield in Rostov, in southern Russia near the Ukrainian border, damaging three planes and three helicopters.
The attacks that targeted energy facilities in Russia and Ukraine followed US President Donald Trump's announcement of an energy truce between the two countries on September 14, although neither side has confirmed such an agreement.
Trump had earlier urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, saying the attacks had caused a diesel shortage that was “hurting the world.”
Since the beginning of the summer, Ukrainian drone strikes have caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia and stoked discontent among citizens who had previously been largely insulated from the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.

articles.title: Iranian arms and foreign components sustain Houthi military buildup, CAR report says
articles.body:
The Houthis pose a threat to the region, and they have demonstrated their capabilities through their recent offensive along the Red Sea. A new report by Conflict Armament Research examines the sources of their weapons and highlights their continued close ties to Iran.
Rob Hunter-Perkins, the Head of Research at Conflict Armament Research, said in a recent report from the group that “external support remains a key factor in the Houthis ’ ability to sustain operations, and the evidence suggests that there is a high degree of planning and coordination on these supplies.”
Hunter-Perkins added that “in some cases, the Houthis are even receiving missiles in ready-made kits with assembly instructions.
Conflict Armament Research has documented these assembly labels, which indicate which component belongs to what missile system, and all of these labels use Iranian missile designations, rather than the terms that the Houthis themselves use.”
CAR has produced important reports over the past decade, documenting the Houthis' various weapons programs and also the origins of their drone and missile program.
CAR tracks Houthi weapons buildup across Yemen
Conflict Armament Research said that it “has worked with partner authorities in Yemen and the wider Gulf region to document weapons, ammunition, drones, and improvised explosive devices developed or acquired by the Houthis since 2015, with our most recent deployment to the country in September 2026.”
Fabian Hinz, a Senior Analyst at CAR noted that “Iranian support has been crucial to the buildup of Houthi military capabilities. Iran has managed to secure a seemingly steady flow of technology to the Houthis and has proven willing to share even some of its most advanced capabilities, such as the Kheybarshekan medium-range ballistic missile, with the group.”
CAR put out its most recent report in the wake of the new advances of the Houthis. Overall, the trends among the Houthis remain the same as in the past. They base their weapons on Iranian designs. They have anti-ship, surface-to-air, and ballistic missiles. They recently claimed to shoot down an F-15. They have also attacked various cities in Saudi Arabia.
“While much attention has focused on the Houthis’ buildup of longer-range strike capabilities, the group has also amassed a wide variety of systems aimed at strengthening its warfighting capabilities within Yemen, including small UAVs such as loitering munitions and first-person view (FPV)s, artillery rockets, close-range ballistic missiles, and anti-tank guided missiles,” CAR notes.
“Crucially, this includes evidence of Houthi experimentation with technology that Conflict Armament Research has not documented in the possession of any armed group elsewhere in the world, such as navigation modules and propellers that may be used in loitering torpedoes, which would greatly extend the Houthis’ ability to attack maritime targets.”
Houthi coastal advances could strengthen attacks on shipping
The new report argues that the Houthis capture of the Red Sea coast “would significantly improve their maritime posture. Using these areas as launch sites for short-range reconnaissance and strike assets would enable much closer surveillance of maritime traffic through the strait and more effective targeting of vessels attempting to transit it.”
Iran has shipped complete weapons in the past. In addition, it helped enable a local manufacturing base. With the US blockade, the Houthis will likely have a harder time acquiring weapons. “There is also evidence to suggest that the Houthis are now using the technological foundation provided by Iran to pursue their own research and development efforts, such as using hydrogen power to increase the range of its uncrewed systems,” CAR noted.
Hunter-Perkins noted, in the recent report, that “Conflict Armament Research has analyzed over 800 weapon components from Yemen in the past year, and the vast majority found in Iranian missiles and drones in Yemen are foreign.” That means Iran also isn’t building most of these items at home, but is instead finding a way to get components from other countries. In fact, the CAR report noted the components come from “16 countries and territories, and include commercially available components.
As much as the Houthis depend on external supply of Iranian-origin weapons, Iran itself clearly depends on critical foreign technology to sustain its production of missiles and drones.”

articles.title: Russia using North Korean laborers on student visas to illicitly build drones, report says
articles.body:
Russia using North Korean laborers on student visas to illicitly build drones, report says
Russia is increasingly using North Korean laborers to manufacture military drones in violation of international sanctions against North Korea, according to a report published by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team on Sept. 16.
The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team is a group of 11 countries, including the United States, that monitors and reports on efforts to evade U.N. sanctions against North Korea and its allies.
According to the report, Russia "created a student visa scheme to camouflage North Korean laborers in Russia as students." The scheme generates revenue for North Korea that can be used to fund Pyongyang's "unlawful weapons programs," the report says.
Russia and North Korea have established an "extensive ecosystem of state-led sanctions evasion activities and corruption," the report says. This includes "utilizing student and tourist visas instead of work permits, adjusting Russian law to allow those on student visas to earn income," and "bribing Russian universities."
An estimated 15,000 to 30,000 North Korean workers were employed illegally in Russia in 2025, according to the report. The majority were "manufacturing military drones for Russia on Russian soil," including at the Alabuga drone plant in Tatarstan.
The report estimates that Pyongyang's illicit overseas labor program generated between $450 million and $800 million in 2025 alone. Each North Korean worker employed illegally in Russia generated an estimated $7,500 in annual wages, according to the report.
North Korea has become one of Moscow's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is the only country to have officially sent troops to support Russia's war, while also supplying large quantities of military equipment, including ballistic missiles, artillery shells and rocket launchers.
In April, North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un opened a museum honoring North Korean soldiers who fought alongside Russian forces in the war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Up to 25,000 North Koreans may be making military drones in Russia. Sanctions monitors say they enter on student visas.
articles.body:
Up to 25,000 North Koreans may be making military drones in Russia. Sanctions monitors say they enter on student visas.
As many as 25,000 North Korean citizens may be working in military drone production in Russia, including at the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan, according to a report by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), which includes the United States, South Korea, Japan, and eight other countries.
The report says North Korean workers enter Russia on student visas under a scheme that allows them to circumvent U.N. sanctions. They can earn up to five times more in Russia than in neighboring China. Each worker earns an average of about $7,500 a year, most of which the North Korean authorities take.
As of late 2025, between 15,000 and 30,000 North Korean citizens were working in Russia, while between 20,000 and 70,000 were working in China. The report says North Koreans working abroad earned up to $800 million in 2025 and that North Korea uses the money to fund its nuclear and ballistic missile programs.

articles.title: Russia Employs 25,000 North Koreans in Drone Production
articles.body:
The South Korean SBS News site has reported that as many as 100,000 North Koreans are working in China and Russia, with the latter employing up to 25,000 of them assembling Iranian-designed drones at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Russia’s Tatarstan as well as Russian arms manufacturing, steel processing facilities, and shipbuilding plants.
The claim is based on a report published by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) on Wednesday, Sept. 16 (MSMT), excerpts of which are also cited by Bloomberg.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Russian Foreign Ministry is said to have issued over 36,400 visas to North Koreans in 2025 – nearly four times the number issued the previous year. According to the report, 98% of visas issued by Russia to North Korea were for “students,” in an attempt to circumvent international sanctions.
The movements of these workers and any interaction with outsiders is strictly controlled. Those who break the rules or attempt to flee risk reprisals being inflicted on their relatives remaining in North Korea (DPRK).
The average salary offered by Russia is around $7,500 per year, which is assessed as around five times that paid in China, most, if not all, is confiscated by Kim Jong Un’s regime, leaving the workers in debt to the state.
The provision of this labor support is yet another example of the cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang that included arms supply and troop deployments in return for financial and technical support for North Korea’s ballistic missile programs – which some estimates put as high as $800 million last year. While much of this makes its way back to the DPRK through its opaque banking system, the MSMT details instances of cash being physically transported in diplomatic vehicles and pouches, as well as by overseas business travelers.
Russian Drone Hits Kharkiv Mall, Woman Needs Medical Aid
The MSMT represents 11 countries, including the US, South Korea, Japan, the UK, Australia, and Canada, and is intended to monitor compliance with UN and other sanctions imposed on North Korea after Russia blocked the renewal of the mandate in 2024.

articles.title: Britain is pushing for air defense coalition to deploy NATO contingent in Ukraine — expert
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 17. /TASS/. Against the backdrop of statements by former Defense Secretary Ben Wallace on the need to shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine, the United Kingdom is calling for the creation of a new air defense coalition, which could serve as a pretext for deploying a NATO contingent in Kiev-controlled territory, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
"It now appears that a certain air defense coalition will be formed under the auspices of the United Kingdom. Such a move is aimed at establishing a military presence and creating conditions for the deployment of a NATO contingent in territory controlled by the Kiev regime," the expert said.
According to him, similar coalitions have been formed in the past – the "coalition of the willing" as a key platform and the F-16 coalition. The current initiative follows the same logic, creating conditions to test the possibility of stationing a contingent under a pretext of allegedly protecting the airspace. Stepanov noted that this highlights the dire state of the Ukrainian armed forces and their inability to independently defend their airspace amid the dominance of Russian precision-guided systems, including Geran drones and long-range ballistic missiles.
"The United Kingdom assumes that these units will not be targeted for elimination and will not be considered legitimate targets by the Russian side. This is a major mistake. Any such action, any such military activity, will be suppressed, and there are enough Geran drones to target all systems--including British ones--that attempt to seal off the airspace over the territory still controlled by the Kiev regime," the expert concluded.
Earlier, former British Secretary of Defense Ben Wallace stated in an interview with the Daily Mail that Britain should shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine. "There is nothing to stop a country shooting down incoming missiles or drones over Ukraine," he said.

articles.title: Russia Employs North Korean Workers Disguised as Students in Drone Production
articles.body:
Russia is employing North Korean nationals in the production of military drones, some of whom are registered as students.
This is stated in a report by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), published on September 16, 2026.
According to MSMT estimates, up to 25,000 North Korean nationals may be working in Russia’s drone industry.
In particular, North Korean workers are employed at facilities in Alabuga, Tatarstan, where Russia assembles unmanned aerial vehicles.
Last year, North Korean nationals working abroad may have generated up to $800 million in revenue for Kim Jong Un’s regime.
According to the report’s authors, these funds help finance North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs.
MSMT also notes that North Korean authorities tightly control the movement and contacts of their citizens abroad to prevent defections. Workers who attempt to flee face the threat of reprisals against their relatives who remain in North Korea.

At the same time, wages in Russia may be up to five times higher than the earnings North Korean nationals receive in China.
This cooperation is not free of charge. The deployment of workers has become part of the deepening military cooperation between Russia and North Korea. Moscow gains additional labor for facilities supporting its war against Ukraine, while Pyongyang receives foreign-currency revenue.
The strengthening of collaboration became possible after Russia and North Korea signed the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty on June 19, 2024. The document was signed in Pyongyang during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit.

articles.title: Ukraine Suffers More Civilian Deaths in 8 Months of 2026 Than All of 2025 – UN
articles.body:
August has been one of the deadliest months for civilian casualties in Ukraine, with at least 372 civilians killed and 2,349 injured, a new UN Human Rights for the High Commissioner (HRMMU) report says.
The report, published on Thursday, Sept. 17, says the figure marks a slight decrease from July, which saw the highest toll on ordinary civilians since Russia’s war in Ukraine began, topping the previous high in June.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This year’s figure – more than the entirety of 2025 within just eight months – is 55 percent higher than during the same period last year and more than double the figure for the same period in 2024, it adds.
More drones, more deaths?
The report says most casualties came from “long-range weapons,” with most documented in cities rather than the frontline areas.
“In August, long-range weapons (missiles and drones) remained the leading cause of civilian casualties, accounting for 47 percent of the total (194 killed; 1,077 injured),” it says. “Most casualties from these weapons occurred far from the frontline in urban centers.”
The spike coincides with Russia’s increased use of drones – latterly the jet-powered variants – and ballistic missiles.
In May, Russia hit Ukraine with record waves of drones, launching over 1,400 in 24 hours. While subsequent waves have seen smaller total numbers, the rise of jet-powered and ballistic drones, coupled with non-stop strikes, has made interception increasingly difficult.
‘It Is a Pity’: China Could Stop the War but Leans Toward Russia, Zelensky Says
The report adds that Kyiv suffered the highest casualties with 31 killed and 106 injured, followed by cities in central and southern Ukraine, such as Kherson (25 killed; 334 injured), Kryvyi Rih (16 killed; 147 injured), and Zaporizhzhia (11 killed; 131 injured).
Totals for eastern Ukraine’s Kharkiv was not named in the list.
“Human safari”
Short-range drones, such as the first-person view (FPV) drones commonly used by frontline troops, are said to be the leading cause of frontline civilian deaths.
“Short-range drones were the main cause of civilian casualties near the frontline (91 killed; 727 injured), accounting for 30 percent of all civilian casualties in August,” it says.
While the report did not name specific frontline regions or cities affected by short-range drone strikes, southern Ukraine’s Kherson – sitting just across the river from Russian-occupied areas – has often been dubbed a “human safari” due to the prevalence of Russian FPV operators targeting civilians.
The city of Oleshky, sitting just across the river, is facing a humanitarian crisis as Russian forces have blocked off all routes in and out of the city with artillery and drones, allowing no aid to pass.
Ukraine’s human rights commissioner called the city a “death trap” on Wednesday and said Russia has refused to uphold a negotiated evacuation deal.
Read Kyiv Post’s August frontline report in Kherson here.
Unclear picture of Russian civilian casualties
The UN report says it verified 4 civilians killed and 35 injured in occupied territories, but
says it is unable to verify figures for civilians killed and injured in Russia.
“According to public statements by Russian authorities on individual incidents in August, at least 85 people were killed and 498 injured in occupied territory and at least 113 people killed and 736 injured in the Russian Federation,” the report says, before adding:
“Due to lack of independent sources of information, however, HRMMU has not been able to verify the vast majority of allegations.”

articles.title: ‘Very Massive Explosion’: Russian Drone Falls 4 km From Poland
articles.body:
A jet-powered drone fell or was destroyed on Ukrainian territory about 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from Poland during a Russian attack on western Ukraine on Thursday, Sept. 17, Polish officials said.
According to Polish outlet RMF24, Poland scrambled military aircraft and placed its air defenses on alert as the drone approached the NATO member’s border.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the explosion occurred near the Dorohusk crossing, close to a gas station on the Ukrainian side of the border.
“There was a very massive explosion. Our aircraft were scrambled,” Tusk said.
The blast was reported near Yahodyn, a Ukrainian settlement and major road and railway crossing opposite Dorohusk.
Polish authorities did not report that the drone had crossed into the country’s airspace. No information about casualties or the extent of the damage in Ukraine was immediately available.
Poland prepares to intercept drone
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk told parliament that the military was prepared to shoot down the drone if it approached Poland and posed a risk of crossing the border.
Polish military aircraft were deployed during the Russian attack, while warning sirens sounded in several eastern cities, including Lublin and Rzeszów.
Residents in central Poland also reported hearing a loud blast. The military said the sound came from Polish fighter jets breaking the sound barrier rather than an explosion on Polish territory.
Poland's Tusk to Visit Ukraine on Friday
Poland ended the military aviation operation and canceled its emergency alert after Russian strikes on western Ukraine had stopped.
Russia escalates attacks near NATO territory
The incident came during another widespread Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine. Earlier on Thursday, civilian and energy infrastructure was damaged across eight regions, with at least 27 people injured in Kyiv and Odesa.
Russia has also recently intensified strikes against Ukrainian transport and logistics infrastructure close to the Polish border, including near a train carrying foreign diplomats and speakers after their attendance at Kyiv’s Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference.
The latest incident adds to mounting tensions between Moscow and Warsaw. On Tuesday, Sept. 15, senior Kremlin official Nikolai Patrushev threatened that Warsaw could “cease to exist” if Poland entered a military conflict with Russia.
Poland, a NATO and European Union member, has been one of Ukraine’s principal military and political supporters since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title: Pentagon, Lockheed to Expand Production of Secretive New Joint Advanced Tactical Missile
articles.body:
The Pentagon announced a deal with Lockheed Martin on Sept. 17 to expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, an advanced new Air Force and Navy air-to-air missile meant to equip fifth- and sixth-generation fighters.
The “framework” agreement aims to give Lockheed a “long-term demand” signal, part of a push by President Donald Trump’s administration to build and sustain a more robust munitions manufacturing industrial base.
The announcement “establishes the framework for future multiyear procurement of JATM,” according to the Pentagon release.
“We will deliver JATM at the speed our nation and allies demand while providing value for taxpayers and our shareholders,” Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Missiles and Fire Control, said in a company release.
A Lockheed spokesperson declined to answer further questions from Air & Space Forces Magazine, deferring to the Department of Defense. A Pentagon press officer also declined any further comment about the announcement.
The announcement should signal to Lockheed and other munitions-makers that a stable market is taking shape, said Mark Gunzinger, director of future concepts and capability assessments at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.
“It is difficult for industry to justify expenditures needed to accelerate and scale up production,” the retired Air Force colonel said. “This is a key reason why this is an important framework.”
Next-Gen Option
The JATM is the successor to the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, which has been in service since 1991.
The radar-guided, medium-range, supersonic AMRAAM has undergone major upgrades since its inception, most recently in 2020. The F-22 Raptor, F-35 Lightning II, F-15 Eagle variants, and the F-16 Fighting Falcon can all carry it, and the Air Force isn’t looking to stop buying the missile even as it looks to the JATM.
The service is seeking $953 million for 618 AMRAAMs in its fiscal 2027 budget request, while the Navy is asking for $673 million to buy 388 AMRAAMs.
The JATM seeks to overmatch the Chinese military’s PL-15 and PL-17 missiles and will reportedly double the AMRAAM’s range and hit targets in excess of 120 miles away, though much of its capabilities have been shrouded in secrecy for years.
In its fiscal 2026 budget request, the Air Force revealed it had bought 144 JATMs in 2024-2025 and planned to buy at least another 112 missiles. The fiscal 2027 request, still pending before Congress, has $1.5 billion in procurement to scale up production, but budget documents don’t list any quantities.
While upgraded AMRAAMs provide an improved strike option for fighter aircraft, the JATM is necessary for advanced aircraft already fielded and those in the pipeline, such as the F-47 and Collaborative Combat Aircraft variants, the FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury.
“It doesn’t make sense to invest in highly survivable and incredibly capable fifth- and sixth-gen fighters and bombers just to saddle them with payloads of weapons that will not survive to reach their targets in a fight with a peer adversary,” Gunzinger said.
Mix for the Future Fight
Though reports on the current conflict with Iran don’t indicate the U.S. is using large numbers of air-to-air missiles, a future conflict with a peer adversary such as the Chinese military is likely to look much different.
“Multiple Mitchell Institute wargames have spotlighted the need to rapidly grow the U.S. Air Force’s inventory of advanced air-to-air weapons, which could be nearly depleted within a couple of weeks of high-intensity combat with a peer adversary,” Gunzinger said.
This isn’t the first time the Pentagon has announced plans for multiyear procurement of key missiles.
In July, the Pentagon announced a similar framework for a USAF program known as the Family of Affordable Mass Munitions, which will produce lower-cost cruise missiles that experts believe will be needed in future conflicts for higher strike volumes.
That deal anticipates 8,000 missiles annually once production is at full strength. Work is expected to ramp up by 2028 with 5,300 missiles produced, increasing to the 8,000-missile mark by 2031.
While the FAMM deal will bulk up low-cost options for the Air Force, work on more expensive but more capable munitions are an important part of the equation.
“Our air forces will have a future high-low mix of counter-air weapons, but it’s far more important to focus on the cost to achieve an effect in the battlespace like countering an enemy air threat than the unit cost of a weapon,” Gunzinger said. “The key is to determine the right high-low mix based on optimizing cost per effect instead of simply chasing lower unit costs.”
Allies and Partner Purchases
The U.S. isn’t the only country interested in JATM—Australia announced $736 million in spending to equip its Royal Australian Air Force with the weapon.
That move, along with potential deals with other allies and partners, could also help reduce missile costs for the U.S.
“I believe sharing production with key allies as soon as possible is critical to improving their interoperability with U.S. air forces and lead to cost-sharing agreements that can accelerate weapon development and acquisition,” Gunzinger said.
Beyond cost savings, having allies buy the next-generation missile for their fleets also gives the U.S. ways to standardize weapons loaders across a coalition and share munitions when needed, he said.

articles.title: China could acquire F-35 fighter jet technology through Saudi Arabia, US officials warn - report
articles.body:
US intelligence officers have voiced concerns that China could acquire F-35 fighter jet technology through Saudi Arabia, officials told The New York Times on Wednesday.
The officials' fears stem from the United States' multi-billion-dollar sale of 48 of the aircraft to Saudi Arabia, which has been pending since November 2025. Similar concerns were raised at the time the potential deal was initially announced.
The US officials said that China could receive the technology either via spying or through its military and security partnership with Saudi Arabia.
A Pentagon intelligence report on the subject, the NYT reported, said that the F-35 technology storage sites should be restricted to US and Saudi personnel.
Analysts in the report questioned whether Saudi Arabia would agree to limiting general contact with the Chinese military and associated entities, as well as removing equipment from Chinese manufacturers from telecommunications and router infrastructure.
The State Department, Pentagon, and Saudi Arabian Embassy in Washington declined to comment to the NYT, while the White House and Chinese Embassy did not reply to requests.
Saudi F-35 deal raises concerns over Israel's military edge
When the deal was first under consideration in 2025, the NYT reported that it had raised concerns over Israel’s qualitative military edge in the region.
Israel is the only country in the Middle East that currently operates these jets, using them in airstrikes on Iran in October 2024 and June 2025.
Since the 1973 war, US policymakers have worked to ensure that Israel maintains its qualitative military edge, with Congress requiring that the US guarantee Israel can defeat any “credible conventional military threat” while suffering minimal damage and casualties.
Eli Leon contributed to this report.

articles.title: Tusk warns of ‘accidental’ Russian strikes against Ukraine’s allies in fall and winter
articles.body:
Donald Tusk looks on during a joint press conference with the Austrian Chancellor in Warsaw on September 17, 2026. | ROLAND Schlager/AFP via Getty Images
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Thursday that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes in the coming months against countries supporting Ukraine and play them off as accidents.
Speaking in the country’s parliament, Tusk said intelligence assessments from NATO, Ukraine and Poland indicated that “the most likely scenario for the next few months” is that Russia will step up attacks against Ukraine and its allies, including Poland.
Tusk said Russia’s aim was to “weaken NATO’s integrity” and convince its members that “Article 5 is more theoretical than practical.”
“There is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles could enter the territory of one or several NATO countries on the eastern flank and cause damage. And the official narrative will be that it was an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to consider any kind of NATO response,” Tusk said.
He also said that “not all politicians in the West, in the United States or Europe are thinking about how to defend Poland, Lithuania, Latvia or Estonia, dreaming of immediately proving that they are ironclad allies and will come to Poland’s aid under Article 5.”
“You know that yourselves,” Tusk added.
U.S. President Donald Trump has on numerous occasions cast doubt on the principle of collective defense.
The prime minister also said that some politicians and political groups in Europe were “just waiting for an excuse” to declare, in the event of a conflict, that “we are not going to die for Poland, we are not going to die for Latvia or Lithuania.”
The warning came as Tusk said the coming fall and winter months could prove “tragically critical” for Ukraine, with Russia expected to carry out continuous, high-intensity strikes on major Ukrainian cities while targeting warehouses, rail infrastructure and other logistics essential to the country’s defense.
Such attacks have intensified in recent weeks, also covering western Ukraine close to the Polish border, as Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones that Ukraine has struggled to intercept.

articles.title: RAF to fight above Britain in huge air defence exercise
articles.body:
The Royal Air Force has launched what it describes as the UK’s largest homeland defence air exercise, bringing together British and NATO aircraft for nearly three weeks of training focused on defending the UK and fighting alongside allies in a major conflict, according to the RAF.
Exercise Cobra Warrior 26-2 runs from 14 September to 2 October and involves personnel, aircraft and command-and-control specialists from the UK, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and the United States. The exercise is intended to test how quickly allied forces can integrate, operate from British bases, sustain complex missions and fight in contested airspace as part of a NATO force.
Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth said: “The return of great power competition across the globe and the significant, and growing, threat posed by Russia to the UK and NATO makes this, by far, the most dangerous period in my 35 years of military service.”
He added: “This is why the RAF is investing in our People and our capabilities – to defend the UK, deter our adversaries and, if necessary, defeat them across the Air and Space domains.”
Smyth said Cobra Warrior was being used to rehearse how the RAF would respond to aggression alongside its allies. He said: “Cobra Warrior gives us the opportunity to practise our response to aggression, ensuring we are testing our defences and ability to operate alongside NATO partners during a real conflict.”
The RAF contribution includes Typhoon and F-35 Lightning combat aircraft, P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft and aircraft from the Air Mobility Force, including Voyager tankers. They are operating alongside Italian and German Eurofighter Typhoons, US Air Force F-15, F-16 and F-35 aircraft, NATO E-3A airborne warning and control aircraft and KC-135 tankers.
The mix gives the exercise a broad air combat and support element, combining fighters with surveillance, maritime patrol, airborne warning and control and air-to-air refuelling aircraft. Cobra Warrior is also being used to test the RAF’s ability to protect and continue operating from its home bases while integrating allied forces at speed, a central part of the service’s Warfighting Ready and NATO First priorities.
The exercise marks the culmination of the UK Qualified Weapons Instructor courses, the RAF’s highest-level post-graduate warfighting qualification. Crews are being put through complex tactical scenarios intended to test planning, command and control and the execution of large multinational missions.
Italian personnel are operating from RAF Waddington during the exercise.
Italian Deployment Commander Major Valerio C said: “We are truly honoured and excited to be here at RAF Waddington to train alongside our NATO allies and international partners. Cobra Warrior represents the premier tactical training environment, offering an invaluable opportunity to enhance our interoperability, refine joint tactics, and strengthen our collective readiness.”
He added: “Participating with our aircraft and personnel allows us to test our capabilities in complex, contested and high-threat operational scenarios. The integration and shared expertise between our nations are what make the Alliance so strong. We look forward to a productive exercise and to flying shoulder-to-shoulder with our partners and qualifying Weapons Instructors.”
German Air Force personnel are meanwhile operating from RAF Cranwell, where the RAF says the deployment is being used to strengthen the relationships needed for allied forces to operate together during crisis or conflict.
RAF Cranwell Station Commander Wing Commander Mathew Thornton said: “RAF Cranwell is delighted to welcome our German Air Force colleagues to the Station for Exercise Cobra Warrior. This Exercise provides an opportunity to strengthen our long-standing professional relationships, train alongside one another and build lasting friendships.”
He added: “Visits such as these are invaluable and we are incredibly proud to welcome them to RAF Cranwell.”
Cobra Warrior brings together combat air, maritime patrol, air mobility, air-to-air refuelling, command and control and multi-domain activity within a single large-scale exercise, with the RAF using the event to test both homeland defence and the ability to operate as part of a NATO force in a high-threat environment.

articles.title: US intelligence warns of China spying risk in Saudi F-35 sale: Report
articles.body:
Berk Kutay Gokmen
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
US intelligence officials have warned that a proposed $24 billion sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia could expose sensitive technology to China, The New York Times reported Wednesday.
Analysts said China could gain access to the technology through espionage in Saudi Arabia or its military and security cooperation with the kingdom, the newspaper reported, citing US officials.
An assessment prepared by the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency several months ago examined China’s military access to Saudi bases and Riyadh’s use of Chinese technology in its telecommunications infrastructure, a US official told the newspaper.
The assessment also questioned whether Washington and Riyadh could maintain secure facilities to protect sensitive F-35 technology, the report said.
It has been shared with several US administration agencies and congressional offices, alongside analyses from other intelligence agencies, according to the newspaper.
The Defense Intelligence Agency issued a broader assessment outlining similar concerns in fall 2025, when the administration was considering the potential sale of dozens of the jets to Saudi Arabia, The New York Times previously reported.

articles.title: EU to Allocate €3.3B to Ukraine for Drones, Missiles
articles.body:
The European Union will disburse €3.3 billion (roughly $3.7 billion) to Ukraine for the procurement of missiles and drones on Friday, Sept. 18.
The decision was announced by EU Commission President Ursula von Der Leyen after a phone call with President Volodymyr Zelensky.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the readout published Thursday, Sept. 17, Brussels was prepared to use remaining funds from the EU’s SAFE defense program – an EU defense financing initiative worth €150 billion (about $172 billion) – to launch additional EU-Ukraine defense projects.
“We want to develop together a European air and missile defence system, building on our joint anti-ballistic FREYJA system, so that we can combine Ukraine’s battlefield experience and innovation with Europe’s technology and industrial strength,” Von der Leyen said.
Defense funding under discussion
In a statement published on Telegram, Zelensky described the conversation as “very productive,” thanking the EU Commission President for raising Ukraine’s security issues in her address to the European Parliament.
“The initiative to use remaining funds from the SAFE program to support new defense projects by Ukraine and the European Union is very timely and genuinely needed,” Zelensky said.
“It is important to implement it.”
The leaders agreed to meet in New York on the sidelines of next week’s 81st UN General Assembly, held between Sept. 21-23.
US President Donald Trump is also expected to attend the gathering.
Major General Nikoliuk Leaves Operational Command East
Earlier this month, Zelensky named New York as a possible venue for a new round of talks with Trump and the US negotiating team, as Kyiv seeks to build on renewed diplomatic momentum following US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner’s meetings in Kyiv and Moscow through Sept. 5-6.
Five projects advance
Separately on Wednesday, the EU ambassadors approved plans for five European Defense Projects of Common Interest proposed in July, covering air defense, maritime security, space, drones and counter-drone capabilities.
According to Ukrinform, each project is set to receive €60 million (about $69 million) in initial funding, or €300 million (roughly $344 million) in total.
The decision is still awaiting a formal vote by the EU defense ministers, scheduled for Sept. 28.
Ukraine is expected to participate in four of the five projects.
On Sept. 8, Ukraine’s Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said contracts are being signed with allies for the supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles using the EU loan. Around the same time, Germany announced it would urgently transfer the PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from its own Bundeswehr stocks, as Kyiv urgently needs them to protect its skies against Russian ballistic missiles.
On Sept. 11, the EU approved a €6.1 billion ($7 billion) defense package for Ukraine, allowing Kyiv to purchase the PAC-3 Patriot interceptors amid a global shortage.
“We have already mobilised nearly €15 billion (approximately $17 billion) to Ukraine this year. More is coming,” Von Der Leyen said.
“My message to Ukraine’s friends around the world will be simple: Europe is stepping up. Now others must step up their support too,” she continued.

articles.title: Democrats' Israel divide widens in House Foreign Affairs
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The Democrats' divide over Israel comes to the House Foreign Affairs Committee
Washington, DC - On August 25, 2026, US Representative Jared Moskowitz (D-FL) was selected by the Democratic Party to become the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee’s (HFAC) Subcommittee on the Middle East and North Africa.
The appointment comes at a moment when many Democratic voters are increasingly critical of US policies toward Israel, Gaza, Iran, and the broader region.
If Democrats regain control of the House after the November 2026 midterm elections, the party would be putting one of its staunchest pro-Israel members in line to chair the powerful subcommittee despite opposition from their own base.
Moskowitz comes to the post with several years of experience on HFAC. During the 119th Congress, he has served as the ranking member of the Subcommittee on Oversight and Intelligence, where he has played a prominent role in congressional scrutiny of the Department of State and the larger US foreign policy apparatus.
Moskowitz has been prominent in his ardent support for Israel. He has notably championed legislation to strengthen US–Israeli defence cooperation and has been among the party’s most vocal advocates for the Abraham Accords, introducing bipartisan legislation in 2025 that would expedite certain arms sales to countries that have normalised relations with Israel and that cooperate with the United States against Iran and Iranian-backed groups.
In the same spirit, Moskowitz has also collaborated with Republicans to stymie international pressure on Israel. He was one of just 16 House Democrats to join Republicans in voting for legislation seeking to force former President Joe Biden to release a shipment of bombs to Israel and has worked closely with Republican Congressman Mike Lawler (R-NY) to halt US funding to UN agencies that expel or restrict Israel.
Moskowitz’s appointment also hands the Democratic Party’s Middle East portfolio to one of its more hawkish voices on Iran. Moskowitz has positioned himself to the right of Vice President JD Vance and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff on Iran policy, saying that his views align more closely with Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR) and the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC), two of the Senate’s most prominent Iran hawks.
Both senators have defended using military force against Iran, and Graham credited himself with persuading President Trump to go to war.
Moskowitz also initially opposed the Iran War Powers Resolution introduced by Reps. Ro Khanna (D-CA) and Thomas Massie (R-KY) to restrain Trump from escalating against Iran, calling the measure the “Ayatollah Protection Act” and putting himself at odds with most of his own party and its leadership.
He ultimately voted for the resolution once the US strikes had begun but framed his support as a defence of Congress’s war powers rather than opposition to the war.
On the domestic front, Moskowitz has built a political record around delegitimising pro-Palestine activism. In April 2025, he reintroduced legislation that would prevent the federal government from contracting with entities that participate in the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, declaring that BDS “has no place in federal contracts” and characterising the entire movement as antisemitic.
Moskowitz has likewise been critical of the university campus movements for Palestine. At the height of the 2024 university protests, he became a vocal critic of such student activism in Congress.
His subsequent legislative agenda has reinforced that position. In February 2025, the Florida representative backed the Antisemitism Awareness Act, which would require the Department of Education to use the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) working definition when evaluating discrimination complaints, including examples concerning certain forms of criticism of Israel.
The IHRA definition conflates criticism of Israel and Zionism with antisemitism, which in practice chills free speech and punishes those who speak out against Israel and its violations of Palestinian rights, while undermining efforts to combat antisemitism itself.
In Florida’s August 18, 2026, Democratic primary, Moskowitz handily defeated his challenger, Oliver Larkin, a Democratic Socialist who had made opposition to US support for Israel a focal point of his campaign. Moskowitz won roughly 64 percent of the vote in the newly drawn 25th Congressional District, while Larkin received 36 percent.
Moskowitz’s victory, however, took place despite a broader change in Democratic voters’ attitudes toward Israel. In a May 2026 New York Times/Siena poll, 74 percent of potential Democratic supporters expressed opposition to sending additional US economic and military aid to Israel, up from 45 percent in December 2023.
The 2026 poll showed that 95 percent of potential Democratic voters opposed the US–Israeli war on Iran and nearly half said that their party was too supportive of Israel. In April 2026, Pew Research Center found that 80 percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents held an unfavourable view of Israel, compared with 53 percent in 2022.
An August 2026 poll by the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy (IMEU) Project revealed that most Democratic voters in the first six states to hold presidential primaries in 2028 - and in some cases, significant majorities - prefer a presidential candidate who supports sanctioning and cutting off US weapons transfers to Israel.
The shift on Israel is becoming increasingly visible among Democratic lawmakers as well. On July 15, 2026, 103 House Democrats voted for Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-KY) amendment to eliminate $3.3 billion in annual US security assistance to Tel Aviv. By comparison, an April 2024 bill to provide additional military aid to Israel was opposed by just 37 Democratic lawmakers.
The same trend was reflected in the primary season, when several candidates running on more critical positions toward Israel prevailed in closely watched Democratic races. In Michigan, Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed won even after the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and its allies spent more than $54 million against him. Wins like these would have been unlikely a few election cycles ago.
Still, the success of candidates openly critical of Israel has not pulled the Democratic establishment away from its longstanding support, even as some party leaders have modified their rhetoric toward the Israeli government ahead of the midterms. More importantly, many establishment politicians continue to take substantial campaign funding from AIPAC.
According to Track AIPAC, Moskowitz has received $833,288 in campaign contributions from pro-Israel groups over the course of his career and continues to maintain close ties to controversial lobbying groups.
Ultimately, these developments expose a widening gap on Israel between the Democratic establishment and its base. By elevating lawmakers like Moskowitz to influential foreign policy positions, party leaders are once again demonstrating how out of touch they are with popular sentiment.
As ranking member, Moskowitz could use his position to preserve and strengthen pro-Israel tendencies in the party, even as more Democratic voters and lawmakers move in the opposite direction.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes two Russian S-400 launchers in Bryansk. The same systems were used to attack Kyiv overnight.
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces struck two Russian S-400 launchers in Russia’s Bryansk Oblast on 16–17 September, Ukraine’s General Staff reported. These same systems were used to launch missiles at Kyiv last night.
Ukraine faces severe shortages of high-end air-defense interceptors capable of countering Russia’s ballistic missiles, making strikes on the launchers themselves increasingly important. Russia has used S-400 systems to launch missiles at Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv, so destroying these systems can reduce Russia’s ability to carry out future attacks.
S-400 missile systems hit
The General Staff said Ukrainian Defense Forces struck two S-400 launchers near Vygonichi in Bryansk Oblast as part of a series of attacks on Russian military targets.
The strikes took place as Russia launched another major overnight attack against Ukraine. According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russian forces used S-400, Iskander-M and KN-23 ballistic missiles launched from Bryansk and Voronezh oblasts, among other weapons.
The S-400 is a Russian long-range surface-to-air missile system designed to detect and engage aircraft and missiles. It was originally designed for air defense, but Russia has also used S-400 systems to launch ballistic missiles for strikes against Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv.
Kyiv Oblast was among the main targets of last night’s Russian attack.
One alternative to air defense: Ukraine strikes Russian Bastion system used to attack Ukrainian cities from Crimea
Ukraine targets Russian military infrastructure
The S-400 launchers were among several Russian military targets struck by Ukrainian forces on 16–17 September, the General Staff reported.
Near occupied Donetsk, Ukrainian forces hit a Russian site used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones. They also struck Russian logistics warehouses in Kurakhivka, Nova Mariivka, and Luhansk.
Ukrainian forces additionally hit Russian personnel concentration areas near Strilkove in occupied Kherson Oblast and Druzhne in occupied Luhansk Oblast.
The General Staff said operations against key Russian military targets are continuing.

articles.title: US Congress approves Russia sanctions that impact China and India
articles.body:
US lawmakers have approved sweeping new sanctions targeting Russia's economy and Putin's inner circle, with Trump set to sign a bill that also threatens steep tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil, including China and India.
The US House of Representatives approved a major new package of sanctions against Russia on Wednesday, clearing the way for President Donald Trump to sign into law the most significant American legislative action against Moscow since he returned to the White House.
Lawmakers passed the measure 262 to 159, following the Senate's own overwhelming approval, 86 to 11, last month. Trump has indicated he will sign it.
The sanctions target Russia's energy and defence industries, President Vladimir Putin and senior officials around him, and the so-called "shadow fleet" of tankers Moscow uses to evade existing Western restrictions.
Crucially for global energy markets, the bill also grants Trump the power to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue buying large volumes of Russian oil and gas — a measure aimed squarely at China and India, two of Moscow's biggest remaining customers.
That tariff provision proved contentious even among supporters of Ukraine in Washington. Some Democrats, while backing tougher action against Russia, objected to giving the president such broad authority over trade policy.
Gregory Meeks, the senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, criticised the bill's drafting, arguing it prioritised presidential tariff powers over binding sanctions commitments. He said he would have supported the legislation had the tariff measures been stripped out, but Republicans blocked attempts to amend them.
Despite these reservations, most Democrats ultimately voted for the bill, while a small number of Republicans opposed it on free-market grounds. Supporters say the added pressure is necessary as Russia's full-scale invasion enters its fifth year with no ceasefire in sight.
Kyiv welcomes the bill but India holds firm
The vote came as Russian drone strikes hit civilian transport in southern Ukraine on Wednesday, killing five people, according to officials in Kyiv — an attack that added urgency to calls from pro-Ukraine campaigners for the bill's passage.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had lobbied Congress directly to pass the sanctions, arguing that only sustained economic pressure would push Moscow toward negotiations. Speaking in Washington in July, he said Russia was losing around 30,000 soldiers a month but showed no sign of ending the war, adding that the initiative on the battlefield had shifted out of Putin's hands.
India responded on Thursday by signalling it would not change course, saying it would continue purchasing Russian oil "through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics."
Russia remains one of India's most important strategic and military partners, complicating Washington's efforts to isolate Moscow economically.
The legislation also targets companies and foreign entities supporting Russia's military effort and extends existing sanctions related to Iran. It follows more than a year of delay, reflecting Trump's general preference for retaining personal control over sanctions and tariff policy rather than ceding it to Congress.
Ukrainian advocacy groups welcomed the bill's passage while urging swift enforcement. "Once the bill is quickly signed and becomes law, we hope for strong US enforcement to finally end the cash flows to the Kremlin's war chest," said Svitlana Romanko of the energy lobby group Razom We Stand.
"Every day of delay is a day we in Ukraine must bury more people."

articles.title: Russian manufacturer Kronshtadt planned to produce 250 Banderol cruise missiles a month while Ukraine estimates output at around 80
articles.body:
In early 2025, Russian cruise missile manufacturer JSC Kronshtadt had plans to reach production of 250 S8000 Banderol missiles a month, according to an analysis of the company’s tenders conducted by the open source intelligence (OSINT) project Nordsint. That is more than three times the current production estimate given by Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR), which puts Russia’s current capacity at 80 Banderol missiles a month.
In February 2025, Kronshtadt issued a tender for the production and delivery of components. Items in the procurement documents carried the designation S8000, the same index used by HUR for the Banderol missile.
The tender listed inertial navigation modules, onboard computers, power units, pressure sensors, cables, and other parts. Ukraine later found the same components in wreckage from Banderol missiles, including the Kometa-M8 anti-jamming antenna and the RFD900x telemetry module.
Nordsint focused its analysis on components that are required at a rate of one unit per missile, such as cable assemblies for the Kometa-M8, the missile’s radio modem, and the mechanism used to deploy the missile’s folding wings. For April 2025, Kronshtadt ordered 200 sets of each of those components. The procurement volume then rose to 250 sets a month and remained at that level through the end of October.
Nordsint said the figures point to an initial production plan of about 250 Banderol missiles a month. If the company had actually reached that rate and maintained it after October 2025, Russia could have produced about 4,450 missiles by the end of September 2026, the analysts estimated.
Available estimates of actual production are significantly lower. In August, HUR reported that Russian manufacturers were only capable of producing up to 80 Banderol missiles a month, even with production running around the clock. HUR also estimated that Russia’s production plan for 2026 totaled close to 1,000 of these missiles.
Moscow began using the Banderol — whose name translates to “parcel” in Russian — against Ukraine in spring 2025. HUR released details of the missile’s design in May of that year.
The S8000 is produced by Kronshtadt, which is also known for manufacturing Orion drones. The missile has a range of about 500 kilometers and a maximum speed of 620 to 650 kilometers per hour. It carries a 114.3-kilogram high-explosive fragmentation warhead.
The Banderol makes extensive use of foreign components. HUR identified a Chinese Swiwin turbojet engine, Japanese Murata batteries, South Korean Dynamixel servos, an Australian RF Design radio modem, and microchips made in the United States, China, Switzerland, Japan, and South Korea.
Another Kronshtadt tender, this one published in January 2025, called for the development of equipment to test Chinese SWIWIN SW400Pro and SW800Pro jet engines, as well as the TJ-800A2 engine made by Xi’an Sky Phantom Power Technology. (The SW800Pro is the engine used in the Banderol.)
Russian forces have used Banderol missiles much more frequently in recent months. The Insider reported that two Banderol missiles struck the center of the town of Pechenihy in Ukraine’s Kharkiv Region on the morning of Aug. 18, killing 10 people and wounding 17. In September, the S8000 appeared almost daily in Ukrainian Air Force reports on Russian aerial attacks.
In early September, Ukraine’s defense technology cluster Brave1 said Ukrainian developers had created a lower-cost system to intercept Banderol missiles and that it was already in use.

articles.title: U.S. Inspects Greenland Airfield Once Considered for Military Base
articles.body:
American military engineers are surveying Narsarsuaq Airport in southern Greenland to assess its potential for future use.
The Danish media outlet DR reported on the development, publishing footage of the military personnel working at the airfield.
According to journalists, four U.S. service members measured the runway and inspected other facilities that could potentially be used for military purposes.
The U.S. military’s Northern Command confirmed that specialists are conducting “technical surveys.” They are collecting data on the airfield’s dimensions, existing facilities, and runway characteristics for potential use by the United States, Denmark, or other NATO allies.
Military engineers from the Naval Construction Force, known as the Seabees, have arrived in Narsarsuaq. The unit specializes in constructing and preparing military infrastructure, including airfields, ports, and roads.
The U.S. specialists were transported by a Danish military EH-101 helicopter. Danish Arctic Shield exercises are currently underway near the airfield. However, the exercise commander in Narsarsuaq told DR that the U.S. team is not participating in them.
Denmark’s Defence Command described the work by the U.S. military personnel as a technical survey aimed at strengthening security in Greenland together with NATO allies. The Defence Command did not report whether the survey was related to the possibility of establishing a U.S. military base.
The Greenlandic government said it is negotiating with Denmark’s Ministry of Defence to keep Narsarsuaq Airport open for another year. During that time, the two sides plan to assess the military’s long-term needs and determine how the airport could be used.
The inspection is taking place amid earlier tensions between Copenhagen and Washington over Greenland. In December 2025, Militarnyi reported that Denmark’s military intelligence service had, for the first time, identified the United States as a potential security threat to Denmark, amid Donald Trump’s interest in Greenland.
In March 2026, Militarnyi also reported that Denmark had been preparing for a possible U.S. invasion of Greenland. According to the Financial Times, Danish troops had brought explosives to the island so they could disable the runways at airports in Nuuk and Kangerlussuaq if such a scenario occurred.
The U.S. military presence in Greenland has a long history. The island is home to Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base. It is part of the U.S. warning system for missile attacks and space surveillance.
Greenland is strategically important due to its location in the Arctic between North America and Europe. The island is also important for Western missile defense, as radar stations located there enable the early detection of threats approaching from the north.

articles.title: At least 19 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine
articles.body:
At least 19 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine
The missile and drone strikes targeted Ukraine’s capital Kyiv as well as the Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions.
Ukrainian officials say at least 19 people have been injured in Russian missile and drone strikes targeting Kyiv and surrounding areas.
Ukraine’s Air Force said on Thursday that it destroyed or suppressed 131 Russian aerial targets during the overnight attacks, adding that the main areas targeted were the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
