- list 2 of 3Why is Trump warning Zelenskyy not to hit Russian diesel refineries?
- list 3 of 3NATO pledges more Ukraine support after Russia strikes near Poland
Strikes were recorded at 36 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at five sites.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces hit metallurgical and electronics plants, factories of the military-industrial complex, energy and transport facilities in the three regions.
Three bulk carriers and a ferry used to carry supplies for the Ukrainian military were hit in the port of Chornomorsk, added the ministry.
In Odesa, seven people were injured, including two children, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. High-rise apartments in a residential building were damaged.
A private residential building in Odesa was destroyed, while warehouses, a nursery school, cars and garages were damaged at other locations, the service said on Telegram.
In Kyiv’s Dniprovsky district, a warehouse, office building, residential buildings and cars were damaged, according to local authorities. A warehouse was damaged in the Solomyansky district, while a warehouse and cars were damaged in the Darnitsky district.
In the Podilsky district, the roof of a non-residential building was damaged, authorities said.
In the Kyiv region, civilian areas and infrastructure were targeted in the Obukhiv, Brovary, Fastiv and Bucha districts, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Administration.
A total of 33 sites were damaged, with the worst reported in the Brovary district, where 14 sites were hit, and the Fastiv district, where 10 were damaged, Tkachenko said in a statement on Telegram.
The damaged sites included homes, warehouses, production facilities and vehicles. No casualties or injuries were reported, he said.
Al Jazeera’s Rory Challands, reporting from Kyiv, said the strikes come days after United States President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to suspend attacks on energy facilities.
“We have a situation where just a few days ago, [US President] Donald Trump announced that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy targets,” as Trump has blamed the Russia-Ukraine war for the rising cost of diesel around the world, said Challands.
However, “neither Russia nor Ukraine have agreed to this and they are continuing to hit each other’s energy targets”, said Challands, with Russia promising to increase its “mass attacks on the Ukrainian energy grid going into the winter months”.
Russian attacks “almost collapsed the Ukrainian energy grid” last winter, with Ukraine’s energy providers now saying that they are “expecting another very tough winter” but hoping that it will be better than the previous one, said Challands.
A Ukrainian drone attack hit an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, northeast of Moscow, said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The resulting fire from the attack had been extinguished, announced regional governor Mikhail Yevrayev.
Zelenskyy also reported damage to Russian warplanes and helicopters in a strike on a military base in the southern city of Rostov.
“There have also been good results in the Black Sea,” the president said on social media, without giving further details.
Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine exchanged the bodies of their war dead, with Moscow handing over the remains of 252 people and receiving 23 bodies in the swap at the Belarusian-Ukrainian border, Belarusian state news agency BELTA reported.

articles.title: Israeli F-35s to Receive SPICE 1000 High-Precision Munitions
articles.body:
The Israeli company Rafael, in collaboration with Lockheed Martin, is accelerating the integration of the SPICE 1000 high-precision munition into the F-35I Adir fighter jet.
Rafael announced this during the Air, Space, and Cyber Symposium conference.
The work is being carried out at Lockheed Martin facilities in the U.S. The integration process is expected to take several months. Rafael notes that in the future, the SPICE 1000 may become available not only to Israeli F-35I fighters but also to other operators of the F-35 family of fighter jets.
The integration of this munition was previously mentioned in official U.S. Department of Defense documentation. In an August report on the F-35 program, the munition is designated as the Israel-unique Smart, Precise Impact, Cost-Effective 1000B—SPICE 1000B.
The document noted that plans are in place to accelerate its integration using the so-called “SPICE Lite” process. Details of this approach were not disclosed.
SPICE is a family of high-precision air-launched munitions equipped with an electro-optical guidance system. It includes the SPICE 250, SPICE 1000, and SPICE 2000. The numerical designation roughly corresponds to the munition’s weight class.
The SPICE 1000 is based on a 1,000-pound (approximately 454 kg) class aerial bomb. After release, it deploys its wings, allowing it to engage targets at a range of about 125 km. According to the manufacturer, the stated circular error probability is approximately three meters.
For guidance, the munition uses inertial and satellite navigation in combination with an electro-optical homing head. During the terminal phase of flight, the system can compare images of the terrain with preloaded images of the target.
Thanks to this, the SPICE 1000 is capable of continuing guidance even in the absence of or when GPS signals are jammed. After being dropped, the munition can autonomously guide itself to the target. Additionally, prior to deployment, the approach direction and angle of attack can be set to strike fortified targets from above.
The SPICE 1000 has been in service with the Israeli Air Force since 2017. The munition is integrated with the F-16C/D Barak, F-15I Raam, and F-15 Bazs fighter jets.
Currently, Israel is the only foreign operator of the F-35 that has been granted expanded authority to integrate its own systems into the aircraft. The F-35I Adir version is equipped with Israeli communications, electronic warfare, and software components and is adapted for the use of national weapons.
In November 2023, the United States announced the provision of SPICE precision-guided bombs to Israel totaling approximately $320 million.

articles.title: Zelenskyy seeks drone deal, closer defense technology ties with Japan
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Ukraine wants to expand defense technology cooperation with Japan, including through a proposed drone deal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday.
In an interview with Japanese broadcaster NHK, Zelenskyy said Japanese companies could benefit from Ukraine’s experience in maritime monitoring, reconnaissance, mine clearance, air defense and cybersecurity.
“We very much want to build military-technology cooperation between Ukraine and Japan,” he said, expressing interest in partnerships at both government and business levels.
More than 70% of Ukraine’s defense industry was in the private sector, he said, suggesting that closer defense ties could also boost bilateral trade. Any decisions on defense equipment would be up to Japan, he added.
Zelenskyy said cooperation could contribute to security in the Asia-Pacific region, warning that North Korea was gaining combat experience through its military involvement in Russia.
He alleged that Pyongyang had sent between 30,000 and 50,000 troops to Russia, where they had gained experience in modern warfare, including drone operations, that could later be applied elsewhere.
Turning to China, Zelenskyy accused Beijing of failing to use its influence over Moscow to help end the war.
“I don’t see China putting pressure on Russia to stop the war,” he said.
He described himself as “vexed” by China’s lack of political support for Ukraine and said Beijing was “a little bit more” on Russia’s side.
Zelenskyy said he had not personally seen Chinese-made missiles in Ukraine. While alleging that Chinese equipment and technology were reaching Russia, he clarified that he was not referring to direct Chinese weapons supplies.
China has said it is not a party to the conflict and has called for a political settlement.

articles.title: From ‘city of camels’ to Israel’s new dream: Beersheba reinventing itself under Mayor Danilovich
articles.body:
“When I was a child in Beersheba, between Beersheba and Tel Aviv it was like light-years,” the mayor told The Jerusalem Post. “They called us the city of camels, the end of the world, a desert city.”
Danilovich, born in Beersheba in 1971 and mayor since 2008, has spent much of his political life trying to dismantle that image. Today, the city has around 223,600 residents and some 30,000 students studying at its higher-education institutions. Ben-Gurion University of the Negev alone has around 20,000 students and says roughly a third of Israel’s engineers graduate from BGU.
Those numbers help explain why Danilovich’s enthusiastic outlook on his hometown suggests a place seen less as Israel’s periphery and more as a place where several of the country’s largest national projects are now converging.
The IDF began moving units into its new technological campus in Beersheba in May, next to the Gav-Yam Negev high-tech park and close to BGU. Around 8,000 soldiers and career officers are ultimately expected to serve there. Northeast of the city, the Intelligence Campus near Shoket Junction is being built for well over 10,000 Intelligence Directorate personnel.
Across the road from the university, Gav-Yam says some 2,500 engineers already work for around 70 companies at its Beersheba technology park. Nvidia, meanwhile, has been expanding its presence in the city, tripling its office space and planning to recruit hundreds of employees.
Beersheba’s tech ecosystem draws global companies
“The companies come by themselves,” Danilovich said. “They are not philanthropic. They are business companies. They come where it is worthwhile for them.”
He reeled off Microsoft, Dell, Nvidia, IBM and Deutsche Telekom before turning to the geography itself: the university, Soroka University Medical Center, the National Cyber Directorate, military technology units and defense companies, all clustered within a relatively small area.
“Show me another city – not in Israel, in the world – where in such a small radius there is such a concentration of knowledge,” he said.
That concentration is at the heart of what Danilovich repeatedly calls the “new Israeli dream.” The Negev accounts for around 60% of Israel’s territory and is home to roughly 1.5 million people. He argues that successive governments have allowed too much of the country’s population and economic activity to remain concentrated in the center, while neglecting the South's sheer size and potential.
“The Negev is not the problem of the State of Israel,” he told the Post. “The Negev can be the solution.”
Beersheba mayor looks to aliyah to reshape Israel’s periphery
Aliyah is central to that proposal. Danilovich wants Israel to set a national target of one million new immigrants over five to seven years, paired with housing incentives, employment, and community infrastructure intended to encourage many to settle in the Negev and Galilee.
Beersheba has precedent for immigration changing the character of the city. More than 60,000 immigrants from the former Soviet Union arrived during the great aliyah wave of the 1990s, bringing doctors, engineers, academics, and a substantial new Russian-speaking community to Beersheba. Danilovich points particularly to Soroka, where some of the young immigrant physicians who arrived then would later rise to head hospital departments.
“When did we become the Start-Up Nation?” Danilovich asked. “When the gates of the former Soviet Union opened.”
Since October 7, he has also framed his aliyah drive around the rise in antisemitism abroad, particularly in countries such as Britain, France and Canada. His complaint is that while Israel has mechanisms for absorbing newcomers, it lacks the kind of large-scale national plan that could take advantage of a major new wave of immigration if one materialized.
“Come home,” he said. “We will receive you with open arms.”
Another part of that thinking is already taking shape in Beersheba. JNF-USA is developing a $350 million World Zionist Village in the city, whose master plan was approved in 2025. The organization now expects it to open in 2029, with plans for educational programs, accommodation and a center intended to bring young Jews and community leaders from around the world to spend meaningful periods of time in Israel.
Danilovich hopes some will stay. He is almost as interested, however, in those who eventually return to London, Toronto, Johannesburg, Melbourne or elsewhere after a year spent in Beersheba.
“Maybe you will want to make aliyah,” he said. “And even if you don’t, you will go back... but you will be a good ambassador for the State of Israel.”
War leaves its mark on Beersheba’s growth
Beersheba’s development has taken place alongside a less welcome constant: war. Soroka, the main hospital serving southern Israel, took a direct hit from an Iranian ballistic missile on June 19, 2025. The government subsequently approved NIS 360 million toward reconstruction, while philanthropist Sylvan Adams pledged another $100 million.
For Danilovich, the cranes that will rise at Soroka are something he has been through before. He was in his mid-30s when he defeated veteran mayor Yaakov Turner in the November 2008 election, after already serving a decade as deputy mayor. Within weeks, Beersheba was under rocket fire from Gaza during Operation Cast Lead.
Since then, he has led the city through repeated rounds of fighting, each followed, in his memory, by the return of construction.
“After every round ended, I would see the cranes in Beersheba,” he recalled. “Suddenly we are building another neighborhood, suddenly the lake, suddenly the amphitheater, suddenly the high-tech park, suddenly the stadium. We don’t stop for a moment.”
The physical change is obvious to anyone who remembers the older city. Beersheba River Park occupies land where sewage, rubbish and industrial waste once lined the banks of Nahal Beersheba; the rehabilitation project now stretches for kilometers through the city.
From football stadium to high tech, Danilovich eyes the next stage
Danilovich has his own, rather less grandiose benchmark. A former amateur football player, he remembers Beersheba’s old stadium as so uninviting that women and children rarely attended, and even decent toilets were a problem.
Today, he can list the stadium alongside the high-tech park, university, cultural institutions and national park River Park when describing how far his hometown has traveled. Yet after nearly 18 years as mayor, he is wary of sounding satisfied.
“A mayor who is satisfied is not a serious mayor,” Danilovich told the Post. “A mayor should never be satisfied, because he always has to aspire to the next thing.”
Danilovich has received many offers over the years to make the move into national politics, including approaches from prime ministers and other political leaders. He said he turned them down.
“My mission for the State of Israel, for my people and for my country is here,” he said. “It is in the Negev.
“If we do not make it flourish, if we do not strengthen it, if we do not build it and make it attractive, if it does not become the new Israeli dream, the State of Israel will be in danger.”

articles.title: Tusk: intelligence sees Russian plan for drone strikes on Poland, allies
articles.body:
Prime Minister Donald Tusk outlined in the Sejm the "most likely" scenario for the months ahead, warning of serious events and hybrid attacks on Poland and other Ukraine backers.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk, in a special address to the Sejm, said he was presenting the public and MPs with "the most probable scenario for the coming few months".
"It is a scenario involving serious events and requiring us to be focused, serious and, above all, mentally ready to pass difficult tests," Tusk said.
He stressed that such tests "certainly lie ahead for all Poles".
The head of government pointed out that his comments refer to the period up to early spring, "because, according to all sources, it is late autumn and winter that will be the most critical phase of the Russian-Ukrainian war so far".
Jet-powered drones: Russia's new weapon
He also pointed to a significant development "of a very negative nature": Russia is rolling out on a mass scale a new type of drone – jet-powered drones that travel at much higher speeds and operate at high altitude before dropping and hitting their target. He noted that hardly anyone is effectively prepared to counter them and that "this is work we, too, have to do".
Tusk announced he would travel to Ukraine to talk with President Volodymyr Zelensky "about how we can cooperate within the anti-ballistic coalition and make use of the skills, capabilities and capacities of Ukraine and other countries in this field as well".
He also referred to the unfulfilled promises of an energy truce previously mentioned by US President Donald Trump.
"Since then, there have been many attacks, including on energy infrastructure in Ukraine. We must therefore assume this will continue, which also has consequences for Poland, as these attacks are increasingly targeting installations very close to our border crossings with Ukraine," he said.
According to the prime minister, Russia's aim is to destroy Ukraine's economy and logistics on as large a scale as possible. "For now, Ukraine's," he added pointedly.
Six main Ukrainian cities in Russia's sights
The Polish prime minister said constant strikes of very high frequency and intensity are expected on six key Ukrainian cities, along with the destruction of stockpiles of supplies essential for the country's defence and of railway infrastructure. Tusk recalled that in the past several weeks Russians have destroyed more than 300 Ukrainian railway locomotives.
The head of government said that "in the assessment of intelligence services, Russia's plans also include hybrid strikes with drones and missiles on states supporting Ukraine, including Poland". Such possibilities have been mentioned for some time, but now, Tusk stressed, the information is already "highly consistent and, unfortunately, persuasive".
In the prime minister's view, potential strikes will be "so-called 'accidental'", aimed at paralysing or weakening NATO members' motivation to invoke alliance provisions in the event of aggression.
"There is a real risk that the territory of one or several NATO countries on the eastern flank may be entered by drones or other types of missiles, which may even cause destruction. And the official narrative will be that this is an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to contemplate any response from NATO," he said.
Russia's objective, he said, is "to weaken NATO's overall cohesion and, above all, to convince NATO countries that Article 5 is more theoretical than practical". Such "accidental" strikes may be repeated.
Tusk: on security, we must speak with one voice
Continuing, the prime minister said that Russia's new strategy also envisages possible political changes in some European countries. He recalled the forthcoming elections and the presence of forces that can be described as an openly pro-Russian option. He appealed to politicians, regardless of party colours – addressing in particular MPs from the Confederation party – "under no circumstances to take part, whether inadvertently or deliberately, in promoting narratives that Russia cares deeply about".
"Whipping up hostility towards the European Union, towards our allies, towards Ukrainians, is directly implementing Russia's strategy. Everyone must finally understand this," he underlined.
In closing, Tusk called on everyone present in the Sejm chamber to "speak with one voice, take joint decisions, hesitate no longer and show that, regardless of political views, we are all patriots in a moment of trial" when it comes to the security of borders, Polish airspace and people's homes. He pointed out that some politicians in Europe "are just waiting for an alibi" so that, in the event of conflict, they can argue: "We will not die for Poland, we will not perish for Latvia or Lithuania".
"Article 5, allied loyalty, fidelity to commitments must become our hallmark," he declared. He added that Poland wants and needs certainty that, in the event of a more serious threat from Russia, it can "count on a swift and effective response from the entire bloc".

articles.title: Scores killed as Houthis, Yemen govt, Saudi Arabia trade attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Scores killed as Houthis, Yemen govt, Saudi Arabia trade attacks
Fresh fighting left scores of combattants dead in Yemen on Thursday, as Saudi Arabia reported its first death since hostilities flared anew and its Yemeni government allies sought to roll back the group's recent gains.
The sides have been locked in increasingly violent exchanges since Yemen's civil war roared back to life, with the Iran-backed Houthis launching a new offensive that saw them capture all of the country's Red Sea coast.
At least 23 government soldiers were killed over the previous 24 hours in missile and drone attacks by the group in two southwestern provinces, a government military official told AFP on Thursday.
Houthi military sources reported 40 fighters killed in Saudi airstrikes and fighting on the ground during the same period.
Earlier in the day, Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency reported the country's first fatality since the Houthis began targeting their territory as part of their revived campaign.
"The fall of shrapnel from a downed drone in Taif governorate resulted in one death, two injuries, and material damage to several buildings and vehicles," the agency said, in a statement posted on social media, adding that the person killed was a Yemeni national.
Images posted by Saudi state media showed windows in cars and shop fronts shattered by the shrapnel, with nearby buildings also damaged.
The incident came a day after Riyadh accused the Houthis of launching a "cowardly" thwarted drone attack targeting Islam's holy city of Mecca, a claim the group denied.
The EU voiced its "full solidarity" with Saudi Arabia as it condemned the recent Houthi strikes.
"We urge the Houthis to cease all military action," said a statement from EU foreign affairs spokesman Anouar El Anouni, adding "the targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure is unacceptable".
Earlier in the day, the Houthis said "Saudi enemy warplanes targeted three telecommunications towers" in Taiz province, with one civilian killed and another injured in strikes on the town of Abs, Almasirah television said.
The Houthi-backed outlet later reported that "three children were killed and several Yemeni nationals were injured in strikes by the Saudi-backed mercenaries", a reference to the country's internationally-recognised government.
The Houthis have been reporting dozens of daily Saudi strikes since they launched their new offensive and seized control of strategic areas overlooking the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandab Strait from government forces.
With Iran already throttling the Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of the wider Middle East war, their Yemeni allies' latest gains cement their hold on the other main shipping corridor for Gulf oil and gas.
The route had been especially important to Saudi Arabia, the world's top crude exporter, which had used a pipeline to bypass the Hormuz and send oil to the Red Sea, which links Europe and Asia via the Suez Canal.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce between the Houthis and the government fell apart after the group allowed an Iranian plane to land in the capital Sanaa in defiance of Riyadh's control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
They also announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began striking its ships and territory.
The conflict in the Arabian Peninsula's poorest country has forced more than 100,000 people to flee their homes, according to the United Nations.

articles.title: ‘You’re Eroding Trust’: What Trump Shifting Tens of Millions in Military Aid Means for U.S. Alliances
articles.body:
The Trump Administration announced this week that it plans to shift tens of millions in military aid from countries in Europe and the Middle East to nations in Latin America with right-leaning governments.
A State Department official confirms to TIME that the department notified Congress that $52 million in foreign military funding for Iraq, North Macedonia, Slovakia, and Tunisia will be diverted to Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, and Peru, and that the funds will be used to “combat narcoterrorism in our own backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal.” The department did not specify how much military funding the U.S. will continue to provide those Middle Eastern and European nations following the shift.
“The proposed reprogramming in the Western Hemisphere will reduce opportunities for adversaries to establish or sustain strategic footholds in our hemisphere,” the State Department official says.
The reallocation of military funding reflects a broader shift in the U.S.’s priorities when it comes to foreign policy. Since Trump’s return to office last year, his Administration has worked to buttress the U.S.'s presence in the Western Hemisphere in the name of curbing drug trafficking from Central and South America and squashing the influence of other nations, such as China, in the region.
The Trump Administration has also sought to recalibrate its foreign policy regarding the Middle East and Europe. A national security strategy laid out by the White House at the end of last year stated that the Administration intended to take a more hands-off approach to armed conflict in those regions and allow them to become more militarily self-reliant. The diversion of foreign military aid marks the latest in several moves Trump has made to cut U.S. troops and funding in Europe during his second term—though in the Middle East, his war in Iran has engaged the U.S. in months of conflict.
Experts warn that the shift in military funding—and the broader plans of realigning U.S. foreign policy it fits into—threatens to weaken the country’s alliances around the world over the long term.
“You're eroding silently, quietly, bit by bit, this trust in the United States,” Jim Townsend, who served as Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for European and NATO Policy for eight years in the Obama Administration, tells TIME of the Administration diverting military funding from European and Middle Eastern countries. “And then when we need them to do something … well, you're turning to a weaker country because you have been pulling their assistance and all of these tools that we have to make them a stronger ally.”
And the Trump Administration’s increasing support for conservative-led nations in the Americas carries its own risks, contends Rebecca Bill Chavez, who served as the Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Western Hemisphere Affairs in the Obama Administration.
“U.S. security relations, these are some things you build over time, and if they start to become relationships only with particular governments rather than with countries, that's risky,” she says. “We have to show the region that we are a reliable partner. And one of the best ways to do this is to be consistent.”
How—and why—the Trump Administration is ramping up U.S. military involvement in the Western Hemisphere
During Trump’s second term his Administration has increased military funding to Latin American countries, as well as boosting the U.S.’s own military presence in the region.
The U.S. has also conducted a number of military operations in the region since Trump returned to the White House, including a series of lethal attacks on what federal officials claimed were vessels transporting narcotics to the U.S. from the Caribbean that have drawn blowback from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in Washington. The Trump Administration has also partnered with Ecuador for a joint military operation targeting “narco-terrorists” in the South American country, while announcing plans for further campaigns of the same kind in other nations in the region.
And in January, the U.S. launched a military operation in Venezuela that resulted in the capture of the country’s then-leader Nicolas Maduro, who had previously been indicted in the U.S. on charges of drug trafficking and corruption. After the operation, Trump pledged that “American dominance in the Western Hemisphere will never be questioned again.”
These moves reflect what the President has referred to as the “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine or, later, as the “Donroe Doctrine,” a revival of a 19th century foreign policy framework first articulated by former President James Monroe that was used to justify assertions of U.S. military and economic control in Latin America.
“Reinvigorated by my Trump Corollary, the Monroe Doctrine is alive and well—and American leadership is coming roaring back stronger than ever before,” Trump said in a December proclamation.
A national security strategy released by the White House in November detailed that “Trump Corollary” in effect as an assertion that the U.S. must be “preeminent in the Western Hemisphere … a condition that allows us to assert ourselves confidently where and when we need to in the region.”
“We want to ensure that the Western Hemisphere remains reasonably stable and well-governed enough to prevent and discourage mass migration to the United States; we want a Hemisphere whose governments cooperate with us against narco-terrorists, cartels, and other transnational criminal organizations; we want a Hemisphere that remains free of hostile foreign incursion or ownership of key assets, and that supports critical supply chains; and we want to ensure our continued access to key strategic locations,” the strategy document reads.
The strategy described the Administration’s plans to back like-minded leaders in the Western Hemisphere as well, stating that it would “reward and encourage the region’s governments, political parties, and movements broadly aligned with our principles and strategy.”
Experts warn about the potential consequences of shifting military aid
Townsend warns that reducing military funding for European and Middle Eastern countries will weaken their ability to collaborate with and support the U.S.
“It creates allies who are not as strong as they could have been,” Townsend says. “It creates allies who are not as helpful as they could have been, and they're creating allies that are not as integrated and as pro-U.S. as they could have been.”
This is especially true, he asserts, for members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), which include North Macedonia and Slovakia. Trump has repeatedly clashed with the U.S.’s NATO allies during his second term, going so far as to threaten to pull out of the military pact after several other member countries declined to help the U.S. in its ongoing war against Iran.
Foreign military financing (FMF) allows other governments to purchase U.S. military equipment and carry out military trainings in tandem with the U.S. Without it, countries may be left unable to purchase key defensive equipment, such as drones or aircrafts, Townsend explains, which in turn weakens U.S. military alliances in the region.
Chavez meanwhile tells TIME that many Latin America nations could benefit greatly from U.S. military support, but argues that selecting who receives that support based on political ideology isn’t sustainable for U.S. relations in the region.
“All of this raises the question whether U.S. security assistance is increasingly being tied to the political orientation of a president rather than to long-term relationships with countries and institutions, and there's a risk there,” Chavez says.
Townsend contends that there is also risk in supplying military equipment to Latin American governments which could use it for ill.
“In the past, the trouble has come when we've been feeding money to a regime that ends up killing the opposition,” he says. “It's been a very spotty record in terms of assistance that we give to countries in the Caribbean or in Central America, Latin America, where this money ends up going to the wrong people.”

articles.title: ‘War without battle’: Europe struggles to tackle mounting Russian hybrid attacks
articles.body:
‘War without battle’: Europe struggles to tackle mounting Russian hybrid attacks
From sabotage and arson to cyberattacks and airspace violations, officials say Moscow’s hybrid actions have moved deeper into Europe
Over the course of the summer, Russian attacks have been pushing ever deeper into European territory.
On August 11, military divers destroyed two drones floating off the coast of Romania near a €4 billion (US$4.7 billion) energy project. Nine days later, Bucharest scrambled two F-16s to take out a maritime drone near the same Black Sea gas platform with hundreds of workers on board.
Earlier that month, German police detected an armed UAV at Leipzig airport, while this week Nato jets downed another unmanned aircraft that entered Lithuanian airspace from neighbouring Belarus, an ally of Moscow. In all these cases, the authorities pointed the finger squarely at the Kremlin.
As Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine grinds on with little movement on the battlefield and thousands of casualties each week, so-called hybrid attacks on Europe are increasing not just in number, but in their recklessness.

articles.title: US clears way for $24.3 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
US clears way for $30.9 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
WASHINGTON - The US Department of State said on Sept 17 it has approved the potential sale of Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Lightning II fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, as the kingdom is drawn deeper into war in the Middle East.
A sale would mark a significant policy shift from the US, potentially altering the balance of military power in the Middle East and testing Washington’s definition of maintaining its ally Israel’s “qualitative military edge.”
Saudi Arabia made a direct appeal for the jets in early 2025 to US President Donald Trump and has long been interested in Lockheed Martin’s fighter.
The estimated US$24.3 billion (S$30.9 billion) sale would include 48 of the military aircraft and 49 Pratt & Whitney engines along with communications equipment, spare parts and other support items, the State Department said.
Washington weighs weapons sales to the Middle East in a way that ensures Israel maintains a “qualitative military edge”, effectively guaranteeing that Israel gets more advanced US weapons than regional Arab states.
The F-35, built with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection, is considered the world’s most advanced fighter jet.
Israel has operated the aircraft for a decade, building multiple squadrons, and remains the only Middle Eastern country to possess the weapons system.
Saudi Arabia, the largest customer for US arms, has sought the fighter for years as it looks to modernise its air force and counter regional threats, particularly from Iran.
The kingdom’s renewed push for what would constitute two squadrons comes as the Trump administration has signalled openness to deepening defence cooperation with Riyadh.
The Saudi Air Force flies a mix of fighter aircraft including Boeing F-15s, European Tornados and Typhoons.
The F-35 issue has also been intertwined with broader diplomatic efforts. The administration of former US President Joe Biden previously explored providing F-35s to Saudi Arabia as part of a comprehensive deal that would have included Riyadh normalising relations with Israel, though those efforts ultimately stalled.
Trump has made arms sales to Saudi Arabia a priority since returning to office.
In 2025, the United States agreed to sell the kingdom an arms package worth nearly US$142 billion, which the White House called “the largest defense cooperation agreement” Washington has ever done.
Congressional scrutiny could pose challenges to any F-35 sale. Lawmakers previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh following the 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, and some members of Congress remain wary of deepening military cooperation with the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia is pursuing ambitious economic and military modernisation plans under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 agenda. The kingdom has sought to diversify its defence partnerships in recent years while maintaining its decades-long security relationship with Washington. REUTERS

articles.title: Saudi Arabia seeking support after US declines to strike Houthis – AP
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia seeking support after US declines to strike Houthis – AP
Saudi Arabia has turned to regional and global players for help defending its airspace against attacks from Yemen’s Houthi rebels after its main security provider, the US, declined to step in, The Associated Press has reported, citing regional officials. Riyadh is running low on missile interceptors, according to the outlet.
The armed conflict between a Saudi-led coalition and Houthi militants reignited in mid-July after Riyadh carried out airstrikes on the airport in Sanaa to prevent an Iranian passenger plane from landing there. In recent weeks, the Houthis have made significant territorial gains against Saudi-backed forces and have intensified attacks on strategic targets inside Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia is in a “very difficult position” because it must protect military bases, government facilities and also oil infrastructure from Houthi drones and missiles, one regional official told AP.
A second official said Riyadh was seeking to rally international allies for a collective response to the Houthis, but added that “the decision now is to give diplomacy a chance.” Oman and Egypt are leading de-escalation efforts, according to AP.
Saudi Arabia has asked France, Britain, Pakistan, and Egypt to deploy air-defense support to help protect it from missiles and drones, the news agency reported.
US President Donald Trump said last week that his administration had declined a Saudi request to intervene militarily in Yemen in order to keep channels open with the Houthis. Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump twice to urge US strikes as Houthi forces advanced toward the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Last weekend, Oman hosted a meeting between US and Houthi representatives to discuss regional tensions, according to AP.
Watch RT’s report on the situation in Yemen, which has been suffering from a Saudi-imposed naval blockade for years.
The Houthis, who control much of western Yemen along the Red Sea coast, claimed this week that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet. They released a video showing wreckage that appeared to belong to a Royal Saudi Air Force aircraft.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia’s key East-West oil pipeline was also targeted by drones last week, forcing Riyadh to shut down the strategic route. Saudi authorities said the attack had originated in Iraq, while Iran-backed Iraqi militias denied responsibility. The pipeline allows Saudi crude exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz and reach the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
The pipeline has become particularly important amid the US confrontation with Iran and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. The US has seen its own stocks of missile interceptors decline during the conflict with Iran, limiting its ability to supply additional interceptors to Saudi Arabia.
As part of its response to the Sanaa strikes, the Houthis announced restrictions on Red Sea traffic involving Saudi oil. Their subsequent advances along Yemen’s western coast and seizure of strategic territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait have strengthened their ability to threaten shipping through the maritime chokepoint.

articles.title: Belarus holds military drills around the Suwalki Gap, NATO’s only land link to the Baltics
articles.body:
Belarus sent tank and mechanized battalions to training grounds near Poland and Lithuania for four-day drills that Minsk says focus on border security, counter-sabotage operations, and defense against drones and light aircraft, Militarnyi reported on 17 September, citing the Belarusian Defense Ministry.
The exercise includes tank and mechanized infantry battalions, units typically used in conventional ground warfare. Minsk says their tasks include guarding checkpoints and infrastructure and defending against drones. Some drills are taking place near the Suwałki Gap, the only land route connecting Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia to the rest of NATO. The corridor lies between Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region, which is separated from the rest of Russia. Belarus denies any offensive intent.
What Belarus says it is practicing
Belarus’s Western Operational Command is holding the exercises from 15 to 18 September under Chief of the General Staff Pavel Muraveyko, according to the ministry’s schedule outlined by Militarnyi.
The drills are taking place at the Gozha range near Lithuania and at the Brest and Ruzhany ranges near Poland. RBC-Ukraine wrote that mechanized and tank battalions are taking part and that the Brest and Ruzhany sites lie about 15 and 60 kilometers from the Polish border, respectively. Reservists have also been called up to local territorial-defense units, the ministry said.
Militarnyi cited the ministry as saying that one unit guarded a water intake, another directed traffic with police, and a mechanized brigade manned a checkpoint with border guards. The ministry also said truck-mounted fire teams were posted around the clock to defend against drones and practiced firing at targets imitating surveillance drones.
Muraveyko said the army was not considering offensive action and called allegations of preparations for an attack baseless, according to remarks quoted by Militarnyi. Belarus has not disclosed the total number of troops involved, and the exercise’s scale has not been independently verified.
The Moscow Times reported that the ministry also claimed the exercise remained below the notification thresholds set by the 2011 Vienna Document, an international agreement requiring advance notice of large military exercises.
How Russia could exploit the Suwałki Gap
In December 2025, security analyst Taras Zhovtenko warned that Russian propaganda had laid the groundwork to cite an alleged blockade of Kaliningrad to justify a limited incursion and the establishment of temporary checkpoints.
A German war game later modeled Russia staging border incidents before seizing key routes, although Baltic officials said the scenario severely underrated their armed forces.
Separately, French open-source analyst Clément Molin found that defenses along the Polish and Baltic borders with Russia and Belarus remained patchy and shallow, with Lithuania the most exposed. These assessments describe possible vulnerabilities, not evidence that an attack is planned.

articles.title: US intervention in Yemen 'off the table' despite Saudi pressure
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US intervention in Yemen war 'off the table' despite Saudi pressure
Saudi Arabia has been pressing the United States to intervene against the Houthis after the Iran-backed group seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, but Washington appears reluctant to enter the conflict.
American military intervention in Yemen is "completely off the table" before November's US midterm elections, a senior Yemeni researcher has told The New Arab, despite Riyadh's calls for military assistance to halt the Houthi advance.
Abdulghani al-Iryani, a senior researcher at the Sanaa Centre, told TNA that unless Iran and the Houthis dramatically escalate the situation, President Donald Trump is likely to stay out of the conflict in a bid to limit potential electoral damage for the Republican Party.
"I don't see a reason for the Republicans to give up their electoral chances for the sake of the Saudis," he said.
His comments come as American and Houthi officials held Oman-mediated talks over the weekend, during which US officials reportedly assured the group they would not intervene in the Yemen conflict.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly urged President Trump to launch airstrikes against the Iran-backed group, which seized control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea last week.
But sources say the Trump administration reached an understanding with the Houthis that Washington would stay out of the conflict even as the group attacks Saudi energy infrastructure and targets its ships in the Red Sea.
The Oman-mediated discussions saw the Houthis assure US officials that they would not target American ships and would uphold the 2025 ceasefire, according to Reuters.
A Yemeni source said Houthi officials also committed not to attack Israeli vessels or commercial ships that are not linked to Saudi Arabia.
The discussions, held at the US embassy in Muscat, involved senior Houthi officials Mohammad Abdulsalam and Abdelmalik al-Ajiri, sources said.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation in March 2025 before launching a two-month bombing campaign against them to halt their attacks on Red Sea shipping. That conflict ended after the two sides negotiated a ceasefire brokered by Oman.
The Houthis and the Yemeni government have engaged in fierce fighting since the collapse of the ceasefire in July.
The group has declared a blockade on Saudi ports and targeted Saudi ships in the Red Sea. It has also struck several Saudi energy sites, including oil refineries and pipelines.
The Houthis last week captured Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline, including the historic port of Mokha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb.
Since taking control of the area, the group has said it would uphold freedom of navigation through the strait but would continue to enforce its blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Few military options
Trump's refusal to intervene comes as the Houthis and their allies in Iraq attempt to shut down Saudi oil exports. Shipments via the Red Sea have been completely cut off after a drone strike last week took the East-West pipeline offline. The kingdom is now reliant exclusively on covert shipments via the Strait of Hormuz, assisted by the US military.
Saudi Arabia has escalated airstrikes against the Houthis in the week since they captured the Red Sea coast. The Houthis have reported more than 450 strikes as Riyadh tries to help government forces retake the area.
But analysts say Saudi Arabia's military options are limited. Airstrikes have done little to weaken the Houthis since Riyadh first launched its air campaign more than a decade ago, and it is hesitant to deploy ground troops inside the country.
Other allies have followed the US in declining to get involved in the conflict. Turkey and Pakistan have shown no willingness to intervene despite the three countries signing a mutual defence pact last month. Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is also unlikely to weigh in after discussing the situation with bin Salman in Cairo this week.
"I don't think Saudi military escalation will help the Yemeni cause or the Saudi cause," Al-Iryani told The New Arab.
"The best bet for Saudi Arabia is to try to help the government hold its ground until the US-Iran war is over, when it will be in a better position to negotiate with the Houthis," he said.

articles.title: ‘More Infantry, More Killed’: Russia’s Next Mobilization Could Backfire, Kyiv General Says
articles.body:
Russian forces have developed an infantry shortage over the past year, and another mobilization campaign would not necessarily solve the problem, a senior Ukrainian commander said Thursday.
Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky, commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, made the assessment during an interview with the national television marathon amid speculation that Moscow could announce another mobilization after Russia’s State Duma elections.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“They definitely have a better infantry [numbers] situation than we do. That is a fact,” Biletskyi said.
“But over the past year, we can conclude that the Russians have also developed an infantry shortage.”
Biletsky said he did not believe mobilization would radically change Russia’s battlefield position because deploying more soldiers would also lead to higher casualties.
“More infantry means more losses,” he said.
The general said the effectiveness of modern military operations increasingly depends on the organization of a reconnaissance-strike system capable of rapidly detecting and hitting targets. Drones and other sensors are central to that system, he added.
Rather than automatically producing battlefield gains, a larger Russian infantry force could provide Ukrainian units with more targets if their reconnaissance and strike capabilities remained effective, Biletsky said.
“More Russian infantry will mean more Russian soldiers killed,” he said, while acknowledging that a new mobilization would still create additional difficulties for Ukraine.
NBU Raises Key Rate to 16% as War-Driven Inflation Tops Forecast
Biletsky also argued that mobilized soldiers could have a greater effect on public opinion inside Russia than volunteer contract troops, particularly as casualties rise.
“The deaths among those mobilized will significantly contribute to social tension in Russia,” he said.
If Ukraine withstands the additional pressure, another Russian mobilization could ultimately accelerate internal problems within Russia.
“If we hold out, I think Russian mobilization could even be positive for us,” he said. “The processes of Russia’s internal disintegration will begin sooner.”
He added that some signs of those processes were already visible but had not yet reached a decisive level.
Former Russian President and current Russian Security Council Deputy Chair Dmitry Medvedev dismissed reports that Moscow is preparing a new wave of military mobilization, characterizing claims of an impending draft as false and provocative, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Friday, Sept. 11.
Medvedev claimed that reports suggesting Russia is on the verge of a mobilization call-up were fabricated to destabilize domestic public opinion ahead of elections to the State Duma, Russia’s lower house of parliament.
“To change that picture, they are spreading nonsense about Russia being ‘on the verge of mobilization,’” Medvedev said, arguing that such assertions were aimed at counterbalancing difficulties faced by the Armed Forces of Ukraine. “I deal with this matter directly on the instructions of the supreme commander-in-chief, so I can state with full responsibility: we have absolutely no need for mobilization.”

articles.title: “I can travel back to Finland and be safe. That is a luxury”: Sanna Marin on the Russian strike that stopped her train from Kyiv
articles.body:
Sanna Marin has made the journey to Kyiv and back many times since February 2022, in winter, summer, and autumn. Speaking at the Book 2.0 conference in Lisbon on Wednesday, days after returning from the September 2026 Yalta European Strategy conference, the former Finnish prime minister said this trip stood apart.
"This was the first time that I noticed so many drone alarms," she said. "I think there was only one missile alarm at that time we visited previously. Now in Kyiv, in this international meeting, I have never seen so many alarms going off when there's an international meeting, also with the US quite heavily represented there on site."
The knock at 5 a.m.
Marin was traveling back to Poland by train when the drone threat reached her carriage. "There was a knock on the door at 5 a.m. saying that we need to evacuate the train," she said. "I quickly put on my clothes and then saw what was happening. But then for some reason we were able to continue, so we never evacuated."
Another train on the same route was less fortunate. "Another train that was also traveling to Poland was evacuated several times, and it was also hit by a drone, and there was a missile that landed quite near as well."
That strike, on 13 September, hit the locomotive of a passenger train near the Polish border, at the Yahodyn crossing in Volyn Oblast. Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said the Russian drone may have been aimed at a diplomatic train carrying security advisers from several EU states and former European leaders, including former UK prime minister Boris Johnson, which had left the station earlier than scheduled as staff adjusted movements in real time. Former CIA director David Petraeus was on another train at the crossing during the attack.
Marin was careful not to assert what Russia intended. "I don't know what are the motives behind this. Was it just an accident where they're trying to hit a gas station, or whatever? So I don't know about the motives." A gas station near the Yahodyn crossing was indeed struck the same night, setting off a large fire.
A warning to Europe
What Marin could say was that the restraint she had seen on earlier visits was gone. "I think it is alarming that there isn't that kind of restraint any more from attacking when there are international people in Kyiv."
She read it as a message aimed at everyone who backs Ukraine, and framed her Lisbon remarks as a warning to Europe. "I think Putin is trying to send a signal that if you support Ukraine, we will bomb you. It's about creating fear. We shouldn't reply to that with fear but with determination."
Russia has made Ukraine's railways a deliberate target. It struck the network around 1,200 times in 2025, more than the previous two years combined, shifting its aim from track and stations to the rolling stock itself, and about 40 railway workers have been killed since 2022, according to Ukrzaliznytsia. Strikes on trains have averaged about six a day since early March.
Why the west is suddenly in range
Trending Now
Western regions were long considered safer because of their distance from the front. Two changes have brought them within reach, and what Marin noticed on this trip is the product of both.
The first is control range. Russia's drones are steered in real time only within a "red zone" near the border and the front, and until recently that zone did not reach the west. Russia extended it by building signal repeaters on towers and rooftops in Belarus, boosting Shahed control signals far enough to reach Kyiv, Rivne, and Volyn.
Ukrainian hackers exposed the network in February 2026, and by June President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was giving Belarus's Aliaksandr Lukashenka one week to strip the repeaters from its border towers, warning that if Belarus did not, Ukraine would. Russia has also used signal-relay balloons drifting from Belarus to keep its drones connected.
The second is speed. Ukrainian interceptor drones had learned to bring down about half of the incoming Shaheds by mid-2026, up from roughly 10% over the winter, so Russia reached for jet power: the jet-powered Geran-4 is built to fly at up to 500 kilometers an hour, several times faster than the piston-engine drones Ukraine spent three years learning to intercept.
Jet-powered Gerans now make up a large and growing share of Russia's nightly launches, and the largest model, the Geran-5, is credited with a range of up to 1,000 kilometers, far enough to put Warsaw within reach of the drone bases Russia has built near its borders. The near-miss on a diplomatic train two kilometers from Poland is what that reach looks like at its western edge.
"That is a luxury"
Marin said she had not felt afraid on the train, and drew the distinction herself.
"Ukrainian people are living in fear every single day. I can travel back to Finland and be safe with my family. I think that is a luxury."
She said she would return. "I didn't feel intimidated or afraid, and I will definitely go back."

articles.title: Indian and Russian army chiefs meet in Moscow as ties deepen
articles.body:
Indian and Russian army chiefs meet in Moscow as ties deepen
Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth is in Russia on a three-day official visit through Friday, where he will hold talks with Russian Land Forces chief Colonel General Andrei Mordvichev as the two countries deepen military cooperation. 
One of the key topics on Seth’s agenda is the availability of spare parts and supplies for Russian-origin military equipment in service with the Indian Army. The issue is also critical for the many upgrade programs New Delhi is running to extend the service life of some Russian hardware, such as the T90 Bhishma tanks.
Russia accounted for 40% of India’s arms imports over 2021 to 2025, making it the largest supplier over that period, according to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute data. In March, India signed a $46 million contract with Russia’s Rosoboronexport to procure the Tunguska air defense missile systems for the Indian Army. 
Seth’s talks with Mordvichev are expected to cover professional military cooperation, training, and other areas of mutual interest. He is also scheduled to visit Russia’s National Defense Control Centre in Moscow and meet senior Defense Ministry officials, including Deputy Defense Minister Vasily Osmakov, whose portfolio covers defense industry and procurement.
📹 India Army Chief Pays Tribute At Moscow’s Tomb Of Unknown Soldier
Gen Dhiraj Seth began his Russia visit by laying a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Alexander Garden, honouring fallen soldiers.
The ceremony was held on Wednesday alongside senior Russian Ground… pic.twitter.com/x67sm8nV79
The India-Russia defense relationship has expanded beyond equipment purchases to joint production and technology cooperation, including projects such as the BrahMos missile. India and Russia also conduct regular military exercises, including the Indra series, which is a part of bilateral defense cooperation since 2003.
Seth’s visit comes days after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin met on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi. The two leaders reviewed bilateral cooperation across political, economic, defense, energy, space and other sectors during their September 11 meeting.
The Indian Army chief received a ceremonial Guard of Honor and paid tributes to fallen soldiers at Moscow’s Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The Indian Defense Ministry said the visit is aimed at strengthening the longstanding defense partnership and military-to-military cooperation between the two countries.
Seth will later travel to St. Petersburg, where he is scheduled to visit the Mikhailovskaya Military Artillery Academy and meet its leadership and faculty.

articles.title: Quadcopters: Israel's weapon for indiscriminate killing in Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Quadcopters: Israel's weapon of choice for indiscriminate killing in Gaza
Since 7 October 2023, the Israeli military has increased its use of drones known as "quadcopters" in the Gaza Strip, after previously deploying them in eastern and border areas.
This type of drone has been used extensively and on an unprecedented scale, are of multiple types, and their use has are not limited to attacking resistance fighters.
The Israeli military has relied on quadcopters in its field operations. Some emitted disturbing sounds or sent messages to civilians about displacement and movement, while others carried weapons. Particular types were designated for assassinations, either by detonating themselves or dropping explosive munitions.
Quadcopters have played an active and significant role in the context of this war, after previously appearing during the Great March of Return protests along the Gaza Strip border, which Palestinians organised from 2018 to 2023.
60 killed
A report issued by the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor on 12 September this year found that the Israeli army had killed at least 60 civilians with fire from these drones or with munitions they dropped since the ceasefire came into effect on 10 October 2025 until early September 2026.
According to the report, Israel has used small multi-rotor quadcopters and tactical drones in the Gaza Strip, which can be equipped with daylight and thermal cameras and systems for identifying and tracking targets.
It said some models can, depending on the mission, be fitted with 5.56 mm and 7.62 mm weapons or 40 mm explosive munitions.
Palestinians recently documented a video that was widely circulated on social media and described as "terrifying". It showed a quadcopter landing in Gaza City's eastern Tuffah neighbourhood at extremely low altitudes among residents' homes, filming inside homes and taking advantage of the absence of windows.
The footage reflects one of the typical ways this drone operates. The aircraft has become part of Palestinians' daily routine in Gaza, whether through its filming operations, deliberate or random gunfire towards areas where displaced people are staying, or the occasional dropping of inciting leaflets aimed at Palestinian resistance factions.
The Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor said field monitoring had identified three main patterns in the use of these aircraft.
The first involved precise and direct gunfire at individuals whom the operator could see and identify.
The second involved dropping explosive munitions on civilian gatherings and tents housing displaced people.
The third involved imposing fire control over areas adjacent to what is known as the "yellow line" by targeting civilians as they attempted to reach their homes and land or carry out their work there.
Ramy Abdu, head of the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, said the group had documented a rise in the Israeli army's use of quadcopters as a tool for precise killing in the Gaza Strip.
He stressed that they had not been used only to assassinate activists or people Israel claims are wanted but had also been used to target civilians, including children, directly.
He told The New Arab that the danger of using quadcopters lies in "their technical capabilities, which allow the operator to monitor the targeted person, verify their identity and track their movements before opening fire, greatly narrowing the margin for error in identifying the target and increasing the obligation to refrain from attacking when their civilian status becomes apparent, or there is any doubt about it".
He added that the repeated targeting of children, displaced people, farmers and shepherds with direct fire or munitions dropped from these aircraft, despite the clarity of their civilian status and their lack of any direct participation in hostilities or any imminent threat, collectively provides strong indications that targeting civilians was deliberate and was not the result of an error in identifying the target or an accidental attack.
He noted that these attacks are "prohibited from the outset" and cannot be justified on the grounds of military necessity or subjected to a proportionality assessment.
He further said that direct attacks on civilians are already prohibited and are not permitted by claims of military necessity or the rules of proportionality, and Israel's use of this weapon, according to the group's documentation, violates the principle of distinction under international humanitarian law, which requires parties to a conflict to distinguish between civilians and combatants.
Abdu stressed that the situation differs from weapons that may lack the ability to distinguish, as "the decision to open fire on civilians despite having the full ability to distinguish them is not related to the weapon's inability to distinguish, which means systematic, deliberate and intentional targeting".
On the ground, quadcopters are constantly present in the skies over the Gaza Strip, including areas where displaced people are staying.
Palestinians in displacement areas see these aircraft flying at different hours of the day and descending to extremely low altitudes.
Use of drones
Brigadier General and military affairs expert Naji Melaab said Israel had developed its use of small drones in the Gaza Strip, so they were no longer limited to reconnaissance and intelligence-gathering missions but had become a tool for carrying out precise targeting and killing operations.
Melaab told The New Arab that these drones are distinguished by their small size and ability to move in places that are difficult for soldiers to reach.
He said that they have been used inside tunnels and buildings in Gaza, where they can film the location and transmit information and images directly to the control centre.
He added that the drone can be operated by a single soldier and has advanced capabilities, including capturing sounds and transmitting them to the operator.
It can also create noise or broadcast messages depending on the mission assigned to it.
Melaab also said the most significant development was equipping the drone with a machine gun that allows the operator to control gunfire with precision.
He explained that it can also destroy itself if it crashes or reaches a designated location, and that Israel has used these drones in the Gaza Strip, particularly for reconnaissance operations, as well as for assassinations. The use represents a shift from drones designed for surveillance to systems capable of carrying out direct offensive missions.
This development reflects an advanced use of artificial intelligence and military technology in the war on Gaza, as the drone now combines reconnaissance, target identification and the ability to carry out strikes, thereby allowing killings to be conducted from a distance without soldiers entering the targeted location, according to Melaab.
He warned of the danger of this type of operation, particularly when relying on inaccurate intelligence.
Targeting a building or home with a drone can result in civilian deaths amid the difficulty of verifying information on the ground before carrying out the strike.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia explores uranium for energy diversification
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia plans energy diversification via Jabal Sayid uranium deposit
Saudi Arabia's announcement on 14 September of the discovery of huge geological resources estimated at 114 million tonnes of ore containing concentrations of uranium and rare earth elements at the Jabal Sayid deposit in the Medina region has highlighted a move towards developing an integrated national nuclear fuel cycle and local value chain, starting with ore extraction and extending to yellowcake production.
The strategic shift aims to accelerate Saudi Arabia's peaceful nuclear programme and diversify its electricity mix, alongside building advanced industrial partnerships with US and European companies to strengthen global critical mineral supply chains.
The technical and historical characteristics of the Jabal Sayid deposit, located about 350 kilometres northeast of Jeddah, reflect complex geological significance.
The site hosts active underground copper mining operations, while recent surveys by the Sedimentary Cover Initiative have revealed deep rock layers containing both radioactive ores and heavy rare earth elements.
The development comes amid Riyadh's desire to move beyond the export of unprocessed raw materials and become an industrial partner capable of producing high-purity oxides and critical inputs needed for future industries and clean defence technologies, according to a report published by Mining, a platform specialising in mining news and international metals markets, on 14 September.
There is currently technical and investment uncertainty, given that the geological data released so far have not disclosed the net quantities of uranium that can actually be extracted from the total mass of rock deposits, according to economist Munir Rashid.
Rashid told The New Arab that developing uranium deposits, processing and refining the ore, and enriching its content to make it directly and safely usable for electricity generation requires heavy financial investment, advanced techniques and high-level technology.
Rashid said the crucial issue in this process is calculating the cost of producing and refining uranium domestically.
He pointed out that if the cost of producing and processing the ore locally is higher than the prices of imports available on global markets, it would be better for the national economy to rely directly on imported material rather than bear operational costs that are not commercially viable.
Processing and refining nuclear ores requires complex technical procedures, including the establishment of advanced chemical and industrial complexes for acid leaching and selective precipitation to isolate radioactive compounds from accompanying metallic elements with high recovery rates.
This would pave the way for processing ores from the Medina deposit and converting them into yellowcake concentrates according to the strict international industrial standards required to operate civilian reactors and nuclear power plants, according to a report published by ChemAnalyst, which specialises in chemical and industrial materials analysis and supply chains, on 15 September.
Reducing dependence on crude oil remains the main economic gain and ultimate benefit for the kingdom from developing nuclear energy, as it would provide additional quantities of oil for export to international markets and generate higher foreign-currency revenues.
It would also directly reduce environmental pollution and carbon emissions associated with power generation, Rashid said.
He added that the discovery of uranium ores alongside other minerals in a single deposit was positive from a mining perspective, but that it was still far too early to determine the kingdom's net benefit before completing field studies, assessing separation and refining costs, and comparing them with available alternatives.
These field steps are complemented by an active diplomatic and regulatory track in Vienna on 14 September, where the Saudi side held talks with officials from the International Atomic Energy Agency and international partners to frame peaceful nuclear cooperation agreements and establish joint safeguards for technology transfers and securing the civilian fuel cycle.
This comes amid ongoing strategic discussions with the United States on nuclear agreements and strict regulatory frameworks for transferring technical knowledge and securing peaceful enrichment cycles in line with international non-proliferation standards, according to a report published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace on 9 September.
The announcement of the discovery of uranium resources, alongside rare earth elements in the Jabal Sayid area, is a promising indicator for Saudi Arabia that strengthens opportunities for economic diversification and provides new sources of state revenue, according to economist Hossam Ayesh.
Ayesh told TNA that the discovery represents a strategic addition to the Saudi peaceful nuclear programme.
He explained that it expands the potential domestic resource base for uranium, particularly as the kingdom is pursuing another parallel route to extract uranium associated with phosphoric acid production in the phosphate fertiliser industry.
Saudi Arabia aims not to rely on a single source but is building a multi-source base to strengthen national energy security over the long term.
The Jabal Sayid deposit occupy a prominent position on the strategic resources map because they contain promising concentrations of heavy rare earth elements, such as dysprosium and terbium, which are crucial for manufacturing defence technologies, electric motors and advanced computing systems.
This places the project among the leading mining projects capable of balancing global supply chains for critical materials and diversifying their extraction centres, according to a report published by Mining.com.au, which specialises in resource exploration and global mining supply chains, on 15 September.
But the discovery does not mean immediate nuclear fuel self-sufficiency, as moving from natural ore to yellowcake and then to ready-to-use nuclear fuel requires advanced technologies and additional processing stages, Ayesh said.
However, he also noted it provides an important foundation for building part of the value chain locally.
Nuclear energy also plays a vital complementary role alongside solar, wind and gas by providing stable electricity around the clock as a permanent baseload, reducing the need to burn large quantities of oil and gas domestically to generate electricity and desalinate water.
This would allow larger quantities of hydrocarbons to be directed towards export markets and provide the feedstock needed to support and expand higher-value domestic petrochemical industries.
The announced industrial partnerships with US and European companies in critical mineral supply chains are significant beyond the traditional investment aspect, as they coincide with Western efforts to reduce dependence on China for securing vital metals, according to Ayesh's analysis of the geopolitical and competitive dimensions.
He noted that Saudi Arabia has an advantage in this context by combining mining resources, abundant energy supplies, advanced infrastructure, a strategic geographical location and investment capital, while Western partners provide advanced technology and accumulated expertise in extraction, separation and refining processes.
Uranium and rare earth elements thus become part of a single strategy aimed at securing energy sustainability, maximising the value of mineral wealth, localising technology industries and strengthening Saudi Arabia's position in global supply chains for energy, technology and artificial intelligence.
This would move the kingdom, according to Ayesh, from being solely a hydrocarbon exporter to becoming a major and reliable player in the clean energy economy.
