articles.title: US Charges Russian Network in Alleged European Sabotage, US Murder Plot
articles.body:
Reported by
A newly unsealed U.S. federal indictment reveals that a Russian intelligence network allegedly orchestrated a targeted attack in Prague in June 2024, part of a sprawling, Kremlin-backed assassination and sabotage campaign across Europe and the United States.
The indictment’s details align directly with a known physical attack from June 2024, when a Spanish-speaking South American national was arrested for attempting to set fire to a Prague public transport bus depot. At the time, Czech Prime Minister Petr Fiala explicitly linked the incident to Moscow, stating on social media: "The unsuccessful arson attack on the buses of the Prague transport company was likely organized and financed by Russia."
Despite the U.S. charges identifying the handlers behind that attack, local law enforcement’s response remains guarded. Colonel Ondřej Moravčík, spokesman for the Czech Police Presidium, told OCCRP police are not conducting any proceedings directly related to the U.S. case and have not implemented new measures.
Spokeswoman for the Czech Interior Ministry, Ivana Nguyenová, declined to address the U.S. investigation, noting only that security services continuously monitor unusual activity.
The U.S. charges target five individuals accused of operating the "RIS Network" on behalf of Russian intelligence. The network paid operatives to conduct surveillance for targeted killings and commissioned terrorism against infrastructure in countries aligned with Ukraine. All five defendants remain at large and face up to 20 years in prison for conspiracy to finance terrorism.
The alleged leadership includes Yuri Khrameev, 63, a former Russian intelligence colonel; his son, Kirill Khrameev, 27, an active Federal Security Service (FSB) officer; and Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, an influential Cuban national residing in Russia. Two U.S.-focused recruiters, Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, face an additional 10-year maximum sentence alongside Yuri Khrameev for murder-for-hire charges.
The Prague bus depot arson was allegedly coordinated by Durruthy, who handled logistics for the network. While based in Russia, Durruthy transferred over $1,000 in cryptocurrency and booked hotels in Poland and Czechia for the physical attacker—identified in the indictment as "Associate-1"—ahead of the operation.
According to reporting by the Czech news outlet Novinky.cz, Associate-1 is Andrés Alfonso de la Hoz de la Cruz, a 26-year-old Colombian national who pleaded guilty and was sentenced in June 2025 to eight years in prison for the Prague attack. Durruthy’s logistical support continued through the fall, coordinating a separate attack in Lithuania in September 2024.
Meanwhile, other network members plotted assassinations. This past summer, Suarez and Castro allegedly recruited a U.S.-based individual, identified as "U.S. Resident-1," to surveil a prominent Russian dissident in the United States, identified as "Victim-1." After paying the recruit for photos and videos, the handlers offered $40,000 to "eliminate" Victim-1 and claimed they had backup hitmen in Mexico.
A year prior, the Khrameevs allegedly attempted a similar assassination in Lithuania. Kirill Khrameev, according to the DOJ indictment, paid a U.S. citizen, identified as "U.S. Citizen-1," $200 to photograph the address of a Russian critic, identified as "Victim-2." Then, "Colonel Yuri" offered U.S. Citizen-1 $25,000 to murder Victim-2 with a "bottle of gasoline" or a knife. When U.S. Citizen-1 refused, Khrameev offered "simpler jobs" like firebombing NATO electrical substations.
"I am offering serious money for serious work," Khrameev wrote, adding he was "interested in all the countries that are helping Ukraine."

articles.title: Ukraine claims 6 aircraft hit at Russian airbase in Rostov
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian forces struck a Russian military airfield in Rostov-on-Don overnight into Sept. 17, destroying one An-12 and two An-26 transport aircraft along with three helicopters.
Zelensky said Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU, carried out the airfield strike as part of a broader overnight operation that also hit the Slavneft-YANOS oil refinery in Yaroslavl, a joint effort involving Ukraine’s military intelligence directorate, GUR, and its foreign intelligence service, SZR. He said the operation also produced unspecified results in the Black Sea.
Rostov Oblast Governor Yury Slyusar confirmed a fire broke out at the site after falling drone debris damaged a transformer substation, cutting power in four districts of Rostov-on-Don. He said preliminary information showed no deaths or injuries, and that the fire was extinguished. NASA’s FIRMS satellite fire-detection service recorded a fire in the area of the airfield’s aircraft parking apron, and the independent Russian monitoring channel Astra separately identified the blaze as occurring on the grounds of the Rostov-on-Don Central military airfield, near the same parking area where military aircraft and helicopters are typically stationed.
The Rostov-on-Don airfield has been a recurring target for Ukraine this year. Fires have been reported there at least eight times in 2026, including strikes on March 28, April 26, May 8, May 22, July 6, July 16, Aug. 6 and Aug. 28. Ukraine’s General Staff also said it struck the same airfield on Sept. 6, along with a Podlet radar station and two Pantsir-S1 air defense systems elsewhere in Rostov Oblast.
“Thanks to our soldiers, who make war tangible for Russia every day,” Zelensky said. “Tonight, thanks to a joint operation by the SBU, GUR and SZR, the Yaroslavl oil refinery was hit. The Security Service also worked precisely against the military airfield in Rostov: the destruction of one An-12, two An-26s and three more helicopters has been confirmed. There are good results in the Black Sea too. We respond to aggression every day. Russia must choose peace.”
Russia’s Defense Ministry had not issued its own damage assessment or confirmed how many drones were involved in the overnight attack as of publication. The exact condition of the aircraft Zelensky named, and whether any were airworthy at the time of the strike, has not been independently verified beyond the fire confirmed by Slyusar, NASA’s satellite detection, and Astra’s analysis.

articles.title: ‘Unconditional’ friendship with US is over – Merz
articles.body:
‘Unconditional’ friendship with US is over – Merz
The era of unconditional friendship with the US is coming to an end, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said, blaming Washington for the deterioration in relations.
Merz, once seen as one of Germany’s most pro-American politicians, has repeatedly clashed with US President Donald Trump over issues ranging from the Iran war to German domestic policy.
“The era of unconditional transatlantic friendship is probably over for the foreseeable future,” the chancellor told fellow members of his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) on Thursday at a campaign event in Berlin ahead of this weekend’s regional parliamentary election.
“We are seeing a change in political attitudes on the other side of the Atlantic, as well as a shift in how the transatlantic alliance is viewed, which we perhaps did not think possible,” he added.
In April, Merz argued that the US lacked a coherent strategy in the Middle East and had been “humiliated” by Iran during the conflict. Trump responded by telling him to focus on “fixing his broken country.”
A month later, the chancellor, who previously worked with US financial giant BlackRock, said he no longer viewed the US as the “land of opportunity” it once was. He added that he would discourage his own children from traveling there for work or study.
This summer, Merz warned the US administration against interfering in German elections. His remarks came as the US State Department launched a nearly $5 million grant program to support projects aimed at what it called strengthening democratic resilience, the rule of law, freedom of speech and the press, and human rights in Europe.
“It was long overdue that we now take more responsibility for ourselves,” the chancellor said on Thursday, defending Germany’s increased defense spending. The country will strengthen its military and continue funding Ukraine in its conflict with Russia despite a “structural crisis” in its own economy, Merz said.
Since returning to the White House in early 2025, Trump has imposed tariffs on most US trading partners and continued his longstanding criticism of European immigration policies. He has also revived plans to acquire Greenland, a self-governing Danish territory, and attacked Merz personally over his criticism of the US war with Iran, saying he was “doing a terrible job” as chancellor.
In 2025, US Vice President J.D. Vance shocked many European officials at the annual Munich Security Conference when, instead of focusing on Russia over the Ukraine conflict, he criticized European governments over what he described as the erosion of free speech and “out-of-control migration.”
Vance also criticized the so-called firewall, the longstanding refusal by Germany’s mainstream parties, including Merz’s CDU, to cooperate with the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD), now the second-largest party in the Bundestag. “Democracy rests on the sacred principle that the voice of the people matters. There’s no room for firewalls. You either uphold the principle or you don’t,” he said.
In May, the Pentagon announced plans to withdraw around 5,000 of the more than 36,000 active-duty US troops stationed in Germany, marking a further strain on military ties between the allies.

articles.title: Russia kills captain of Tanzanian-flagged ship in latest attack on civilian shipping in Black Sea
articles.body:
Russia killed the captain of a Tanzanian-flagged civilian vessel and wounded three crew members in a drone strike in the Black Sea on 17 September, Ukraine’s Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport said.
The ministry said Russia is “systematically attacking Ukrainian ports, port infrastructure and civilian commercial vessels,” threatening both people and international shipping in the Black Sea.
The vessel was heading toward one of Ukraine’s ports when it was attacked. The condition of the ship is still being assessed.
Foreign vessels repeatedly targeted
The latest attack follows a series of Russian strikes on foreign-flagged vessels serving Ukrainian ports.
In July, Russia struck the Turkish-owned bulk carrier GOLDEN LEO with cruise missiles as it left Odesa carrying grain, killing 10 people.
Russia also attacked two foreign-flagged cargo ships with drones in June, killing one sailor and injuring five others as the vessels were leaving Ukrainian ports.
In August, a Russian strike on port infrastructure in Odesa damaged a Togo-flagged civilian vessel and injured four people.
Attacks threaten Ukraine’s maritime trade
The repeated attacks have also disrupted Ukraine’s maritime trade route.
In July, Russian strikes on civilian cargo ships brought traffic through the Black Sea corridor close to a standstill at the height of the harvest, with shipowners temporarily stopping vessels from entering Ukrainian ports.
The Ukrainian ministry called for an international response and coordinated action to strengthen the protection of civilian shipping and the security of international logistics routes.

articles.title: France’s Le Pen rules out more money for Ukraine
articles.body:
PARIS — French presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen is open to continue providing defensive military gear to Ukraine but is against sending money to the war-torn country.
“Given the extent of what we've done so far — which is considerable — we're saying we can't do it,” the far-right National Rally leader said on TV channel LCI Wednesday evening.
“This is not an act of hostility toward Ukraine. We can continue to train their soldiers and their armed forces, and we can continue to provide them with equipment so they can defend themselves. But financially, we can’t do it anymore,” she said.
Advertisement
Le Pen is leading the polls ahead of a high-stakes presidential election next spring to replace Emmanuel Macron. One of the campaign's main issues is France's increasingly strained finances, with a public deficit that could exceed 5% this year.
France's direct financial aid to Ukraine is actually quite limited but the National Rally has long been against the EU's €90 billion loan to Kyiv, which is guaranteed by the bloc's budget, fed by national contributions.
National Rally officials privately say that Ukraine will never be able to repay the EU loan and it will ultimately fall on the bloc's capitals to do so.
"You can't say, on the one hand, that there isn't a single euro … to adjust pensions for inflation, but, on the other hand, that there are billions for the net contribution to the European Union," Le Pen said.
While the National Rally is internally divided over Russia, Ukraine and NATO, Le Pen's rivals have on multiple occasions accused her party of playing into the Kremlin’s hands in order to undermine the National Rally's credibility. The media has also repeatedly asked top party figures to clarify the party's line on assistance to Kyiv.
In Wednesday evening's interview, Le Pen stressed that France under her presidency would organize a conference for peace that would bring Russia, Ukraine and other European countries such as Germany and Poland to the table. The goal, she said, is to put an end to the war.
She also pushed back against proposals made by her presidential rivals, such as former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, to protect Ukraine's skies with French fighter jets — an option Paris has also so far refused to contemplate. "That would make us co-belligerents," Le Pen told LCI.

articles.title: Iran school bombing: grounds to believe US was behind atrocity, UN finds
articles.body:
A UN fact-finding mission has determined there are reasonable grounds to believe the US was behind military strikes on a school and a sports facility in Iran in February that killed 120 children, and that these constituted war crimes.
The school strike, which killed 156 civilians including 120 children, involved a US Tomahawk missile that collapsed the roof of the Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school, which the UN said was “clearly identifiable”, in Minab, Hormozgan province, on 28 February.
The Pentagon’s own secretive investigation into the incident is understood to have concluded several months ago. There have been reports that senior US commanders had been warned that targeting data used during the war – including for the Minab strike – was dangerously outdated.
The second cited strike, on the same date, targeted a “clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area” in the southern city of Lamerd with a weapon that scattered tungsten pellets.
The UN fact-finding team said in a statement: “Following the United States and Israeli attacks on 28 February, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects.”
The mission also found Iranian authorities had committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings by the independent international fact-finding mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN human rights council in Geneva, examined the US’s conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government’s response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.
US officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
The UN mission concluded that the strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law.
According to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike.
Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
“Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen.”
In June the US president, Donald Trump, said “nobody” had purposely attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. The Pentagon has since elevated the inquiry, but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence it was being used for military purposes.
The experts reached a similar conclusion over the strike on the sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack had damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike had been indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
US Central Command said in a statement in March that US forces had not launched any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
The UN mission also found that the Iranian authorities had carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shia Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed “terrorists and rioters” backed by exiled opponents and the US and Israel.
The investigation said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was probably far higher than official figures, which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people injured.
The government’s response to the protests, including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty, marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

articles.title: Britain contracts drone-ship sensors to track air threats
articles.body:
Project HORUS, the Royal Navy effort to deploy persistent air-search sensors on uncrewed maritime platforms, is now under contract as the service moves ahead with a distributed system intended to detect and track airborne threats.
The status of the project was confirmed in a written parliamentary answer from Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard, following a question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty asking for the scope of the programme.
Pollard said: “Project HORUS is supporting urgent operational requirements for a rapidly procured, persistent air-search capability using uncrewed maritime platforms fitted with sensors to detect, track, identify and report airborne threats. The project is on contract and is intended to help the Royal Navy generate distributed sensing that reduces risk to personnel, and will inform future procurement decisions.”
The confirmation represents a step forward from the market-engagement stage reported by the UK Defence Journal in March, when the Navy was seeking mature systems that could be brought into service at pace. At that point, the requirement called for “a rapidly procured and persistent air search capability” able to detect, track, identify and report threats including drones, fast jets and cruise missiles from sensors carried aboard maritime platforms.
The original market notice envisaged moving rapidly from industry engagement to an initial capability. It stated that the intention was to select credible solutions, place contracts and deliver the first capability within four to six months, with an emphasis on mature products and suppliers able to work quickly.
HORUS is built around distributing sensors across multiple lower-cost uncrewed platforms rather than relying entirely on crewed ships or a small number of high-value assets.
The earlier requirement described a “System of System Approach” intended to introduce greater mass through numerous lower-cost sensors operating from uncrewed platforms in areas where sending personnel could carry greater risk. Persistence was also central to the concept. The March requirement sought platforms capable of remaining on station for 30 days as a threshold requirement and as long as 90 days as an objective, without in-person human intervention or maintenance.
The performance targets outlined during that earlier market engagement included the detection of NATO Class 2 uncrewed aircraft, anti-ship and land-attack cruise missiles and third and fourth-generation fighter-bombers at distances of at least 15 nautical miles.
Industry was also asked to consider how the system could eventually be expanded to detect surface threats, including fast attack craft and uncrewed vessels. The initial requirement envisaged persistent surveillance across an area of around 2,500 square kilometres, pointing towards several sensor-carrying platforms operating together rather than a single picket.
Alternative commercial approaches were also being considered, including what the Navy described as “SENSE as a service”, potentially allowing industry to provide the sensing effect rather than Defence purchasing every element outright.
Those figures and performance requirements were set out during the earlier market-engagement phase and do not necessarily describe the final contracted configuration. Pollard’s latest answer confirms, however, that HORUS has moved beyond that initial stage and is now on contract in support of an urgent operational requirement.

articles.title: How to Govern the Existential Risk of AI
articles.body:
The current state of paralysis when it comes to the governance of frontier AI technology is causing tangible harm today and raising the odds of catastrophe tomorrow.
That paralysis has been excused by a dangerous set of narratives: that the technology moves too fast for oversight, that companies can self-regulate, and that in a contest between the U.S. and China, public safety can wait. Governments have struggled to give AI risks the attention they demand. Many are wary of acting alone amid both great power rivalry and intra-industry arms race dynamics. In this context, every call for restraint meets the same reply: why should we slow down if our competitor will not?
But recent events have tested these excuses. Over the past few months, AI agents were found hacking into other companies' databases and seeking to deceive real individuals, while researchers used AI to create new viruses for the first time. And just last week, AI industry whistleblowers made global headlines warning that companies are “gambling with our lives" as they rush toward self-improving models, and Anthropic revealed it blocked users who could have been seeking to design biological weapons.
It is true that there are many unknowns about the capabilities of the most powerful AI systems built to date—as well as those still under development. But what we do know is that AI derives both its strengths and its flaws from our own human intelligence, which is what, ironically, makes strict guardrails necessary. Its risks do not halt at any border, and no country can hold the line alone. We cannot wait for perfect information, nor can we wait for the rivalry between great powers to soften before we act. The need for international cooperation around AI safety is urgent and undeniable.
Between the two of us, we have spent decades driving global cooperation to address our collective challenges and risks—from chemical weapons to climate change.
We have been told before that certain dangers were too complex to control or the mistrust too deep: that the ozone layer would never recover, that smallpox would never be eradicated, that nuclear and chemical weapons could never be contained. Determined multilateral engagement proved otherwise, producing the Montreal Protocol, the smallpox eradication campaign, the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), and the Chemical Weapons Convention. None of these efforts were perfect, and none is a fully closed chapter, but each showed that international coordination on existential threats is possible even where trust is absent.
That is the lesson for this moment: coordination on existential threats has never required ideological alignment or friendship. It has required rivals to recognize a danger greater than their rivalry.
Looking to the past to co-build the future
The NPT's basic bargain—that states forgo dangerous nuclear weapons capability in exchange for access to beneficial technology and a seat at the table—offers a starting template for AI. Compute and model access could plausibly be traded for compliance, much as enriched uranium and reactor technology once were.
The Chemical Weapons Convention offers another instructive model: a treaty that achieved near-universal membership, backed by a technical verification body—the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons—capable of inspecting declared facilities and building confidence precisely because its judgments were seen as neutral, not political.
For the AI companies themselves, a binding, verifiable floor on safety is not a threat. It is the one assurance they cannot manufacture alone: proof, credible to the public and to competitors alike, that the race to build ever more powerful systems is not also a race to cut corners.
No single historical model for international cooperation can be transplanted onto AI. But there is a great deal to draw from, including the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the OPCW, and the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO).
We need an international agency for frontier AI—one that can verify that the world's most powerful systems are safe, remain under human control, and prevent crises.
Such an agency should be the place where serious AI incidents and near misses are reported and monitored across borders, so that a failure inside one company or one country becomes a warning the whole world can act on. It should allow governments and companies to share what they are learning about the capabilities and risks of these systems. From that foundation, the agency should have the power that matters most: to verify safety independently, and, where safety cannot be demonstrated against agreed “red lines,” to require that development pause until it can.
This is not a call for panic. It is a call for political courage and leadership those earlier treaties demanded: the will to act before catastrophe forces our hand rather than after it. We cannot wait for AI's “Chernobyl moment.”
The declarations and calls to action have piled up, the evidence is in, and the incidents are mounting. The moment to break the paralysis is now. We call on world leaders to rise to the occasion: to commit now to negotiating an international agency for frontier AI.

articles.title: The EU has billions in unspent defense funds. It wants to use them for projects with Ukraine
articles.body:
The EU plans to use money remaining under its €150 billion Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program to create a new program for joint projects with Ukrainian companies, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on 16 September. She announced the plan during her State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.
Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine has pushed the EU to spend more on defense and build up its own weapons industry. SAFE was created as part of that effort, giving EU member states €150 billion in loans for defense spending. Ukraine is also facing heavy defense costs, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy putting its additional defense funding gap for 2026 at $27 billion.
"Using the remaining funds from SAFE, we will be setting up a new programme for joint projects with Ukrainian companies," von der Leyen told the European Parliament.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius estimated that the unused portion of SAFE could amount to €10 billion to €20 billion, UNN reported. The exact sum will be known only after member states report on their SAFE projects by the end of October. The announcement caught several governments off guard: Poland and other capitals say the Commission never discussed it with them, and Warsaw had been counting on taking up the funds other countries declined for its own projects.
The proposal would allow unused money from member states' SAFE allocations to be redirected to joint projects with Ukrainian firms. One likely destination is Freya, the joint European-Ukrainian air and missile defense system meant as a cheaper answer to the American Patriot, which von der Leyen described as the start of the collaboration rather than the end of it.
In 2025, Ukraine gained associate partner status in SAFE and access to the EU's European Defense Fund, allowing Ukrainian companies to compete for contracts and co-develop military systems with European firms.
Fifteen member states have since said they plan to buy Ukrainian weapons through the program, and Canada joined it in December 2025 as the first non-European partner. Bulgaria agreed SAFE-funded joint weapons production with Ukraine in March 2026.
The war is costing Ukraine more every year, the government says. Its draft 2027 budget proposes ₴4.885 trillion ($110 billion) for defense needs, nearly 44% of GDP.

articles.title: ‘Reasonable grounds’ to believe US committed war crimes in Iran – UN
articles.body:
‘Reasonable grounds’ to believe US committed war crimes in Iran – UN
A UN fact-finding mission has found reasonable grounds to believe the US committed war crimes by carrying out indiscriminate strikes on civilian targets in Iran, according to a new report.
The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran released its findings to the UN Human Rights Council on Thursday, focusing in part on two strikes it described as “emblematic” of the conflict and involving “significant violations” of international law.
The first was the February 28 double strike on an elementary school in Minab. The mission said credible information confirmed 157 deaths, including 123 children aged 13 and younger.
Investigators identified the weapon as a Tomahawk Land Attack Missile (TLAM), used only by the US during the conflict. Citing evidence including internal Pentagon investigations and Washington’s failure to explain the incident, the mission concluded that the school had been deliberately targeted, apparently on the basis of outdated intelligence.
The site had been part of an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) compound before 2016, but the school had been separated from the military facility by a wall for more than a decade. Investigators said it was clearly identifiable as a civilian site and found no evidence it was being used for military purposes.
The second incident involved a strike on a sports complex and surrounding residential area in Lamerd, Fars Province. The mission said the attack killed and injured 22 civilians and damaged nearby homes and a school.
Investigators said a US-made Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) detonated in the air, dispersing around 180,000 tungsten pellets over a wide area.
In both cases, the mission concluded that US conduct went beyond negligence and amounted to the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack resulting in civilian deaths, injuries or damage to civilian property. It said the US had failed to adequately verify targeting information despite the risk to civilians.
The report also cited rhetoric from senior US officials, including President Donald Trump and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, which investigators said indicated a “deprioritization of civilian harm mitigation” and compliance with international humanitarian law.
Hegseth had called for the US military to be “more lethal” and said American forces would give “no quarter” to their enemies, drawing criticism from lawmakers and legal experts over the implications for prisoners of war.
Trump has repeatedly criticized the UN, accusing it of failing to resolve international conflicts and of bias against Israel, which joined the US in launching the war against Iran. His administration has also withdrawn Washington from several UN bodies and agencies.
The fact-finding mission separately accused Iranian authorities of serious violations during their 2025-2026 crackdown on mass protests, concluding that some abuses amounted to crimes against humanity.
Trump publicly backed the protesters and offered them US protection, while Tehran accused Washington of supporting unrest as part of a failed regime-change effort.

articles.title: A war-fatigued and anxious Russia picks a new parliament
articles.body:
A war-fatigued and anxious Russia picks a new parliament
September 17, 2026
Russians are increasingly anxious. Nearly half of those surveyed by state pollster FOM say a sense of alarm is the prevailing mood among the people around them.
According to data by independent pollster ExtremeScan, 60% of Russians believe that the war against Ukraine has had negative consequences for their day-to-day lives.
"Anxiety and war fatigue are driven by increasing uncertainty," Margarita Zavadskaya, a sociologist and senior research fellow at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs in Helsinki, told DW.
She says this year has seen a shift in public opinion. Rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and rumors of another mobilization drive are making it harder for Russians to plan for the future. Some are even leaving the country, afraid they could be drafted after the elections.
Sociologist and the founder of ExtremeScan Elena Koneva said people were starting to ask the question: "How much does this war cost me and my family? And am I ready to pay this price? "
That could pose a problem for the Kremlin.
From September 18 to 20, Russians are voting for a new parliament (the State Duma) for the first time since 2022. It's the first parliamentary election to take place in Russia during the Ukraine war. And although there are unlikely to be any surprises in the official results, the Kremlin will be closely monitoring turnout.
Why are these elections important for the Kremlin?
"The Kremlin is confident it can fabricate whatever figures it needs. The question is how high of a price it will have to pay," said Zavadskaya.
Although elections in authoritarian systems like that of Russian President Vladimir Putin have little to do with democratic change, they still serve an important purpose. They are a reality check on whether the population remains loyal. And for Putin, that is especially important right now.
"They are crucial for him because they demonstrate that the majority supports the main party, the party of war, and that he has legitimacy for further escalation and the continuation of this war," Russian opposition politician in exile Ilya Yashin told DW.
In the fifth year of the war in Ukraine, there is little sign the Kremlin is willing to end the conflict. United Russia, a party de facto led by Putin, is campaigning on a platform that lists victory in the war among its priorities. Its candidate list is headed by people presented as veterans of the war against Ukraine.
But many Russians appear to want the opposite.
"The silent majority just wants the war to end," opposition politician Yulia Galyamina, who still lives in Russia, said in a recent interview with online media-outlet Bereg. Most of these people still support Putin, but they are becoming increasingly anti-war, she said.
That mood is also reflected in polling. Six in 10 Russians favor peace negotiations with Ukraine, according to independent pollster Levada Center. Recent Kremlin hints at a new round of peace talks in October may be a tactic to calm the electorate, Zavadskaya said.
Support for Yabloko has been rising
One party has sought to capitalize on this anti-war sentiment: Yabloko.
The liberal opposition party is the only registered political force opposing the war in Ukraine.
Although its rating was below 5% in July, the party has seen a surge in popularity since then. Many people, especially younger Russians, are joining Yabloko and volunteering.
According to the independent pollster ExtremeScan, 18% of Russians would have voted for Yabloko. But they will not be able to: In a recent court decision, Yabloko was barred from running in the parliamentary elections.
"This support for Yabloko is, in fact, a demonstration of people's attitude toward the war," Koneva told DW.
What will anti-war voters do?
Now, with Yabloko out of the race, are there still ways for Russians to express that attitude?
Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of Alexei Navalny, and opposition politician in exile Maxim Katz are urging supporters to back any party except United Russia in an effort to reduce the ruling party's result in the election.
Yabloko has taken a different approach, encouraging voters to spoil their ballots.
Yashin says neither choice matters. What matters, he says, is showing up at polling stations at noon on Sept. 20.
"These queues will be a visible expression of public discontent," he said. "No need for flags, banners, or symbols. Everyone will know: the queues at noon are made up of people who do not want the war to continue."
DW Russian asked its readers anonymously whether they plan to vote in the upcoming election. Most of those who responded said they would follow Navalnaya's and Katz's advice.
"Elections have long become a farce and a political spectacle. But I will vote because I want to show that I have a position," one user said.
Others decided to stay away from the elections. One respondent wrote: "I don't want to legitimize Putin's regime."
Sergei Satanovskii contributed reporting.
Edited by: Carla Bleiker

articles.title: Iran downed at least 2 American drones in recent days, U.S. officials say
articles.body:
Iran downed at least 2 unmanned American aircraft in recent days, U.S. officials say
Washington — Iranian forces in recent days have brought down at least two American MQ-1 unmanned aircraft, according to U.S. officials familiar with the matter who spoke to CBS News on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
It is unclear where in the region the remotely piloted aircraft were brought down or which MQ-1 variant was involved. The U.S. military has fielded two principal MQ-1 variants: the Predator, which became a fixture of U.S. operations in Iraq and Afghanistan before the Air Force retired it in 2018, and the Gray Eagle, a larger Predator-derived aircraft still operated by the Army, including its special operations forces.
Both the Predator and Gray Eagle were designed for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions but they can also carry Hellfire missiles for striking targets. In the Strait of Hormuz, these unmanned aircraft can provide U.S. forces with persistent surveillance over the narrow waterway while also tracking Iranian military activity and monitoring threats to both American forces and commercial shipping.
If the aircraft were the Air Force's older MQ-1 Predators that have largely been retired, the loss of two would equate to roughly $8 million total. Gray Eagles are more expensive depending on the variant and can cost tens of millions of dollars.
At least 24 MQ-9 Reapers have been lost since the U.S. began its war with Iran, representing a loss of roughly $720 million, according to a report released by the Congressional Budget Office this week. The report also said an MQ-4C Triton was destroyed, a loss of about $150 million.
U.S. Central Command, the U.S. military unit responsible for operations against Iran, declined to comment to CBS News on Thursday.

articles.title: Why is Trump shifting millions in military aid to South America?
articles.body:
Why is Trump shifting millions in military aid to South America?
The US has decided to redirect $52 million in foreign military financing to four countries in South America, the Associated Press reported on Tuesday.
The funds, which subsidize purchases of American military equipment, are being reallocated from Slovakia, North Macedonia, Tunisia, and Iraq to Panama, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia, the news agency said, citing a State Department notification to Congress.
The shift comes as US President Donald Trump has placed greater emphasis on the Western Hemisphere under what he has called the ‘Donroe Doctrine’, his version of the 19th-century hegemonic Monroe Doctrine. The Trump administration has said it intends to strengthen US influence in the Americas while preventing rival powers from gaining strategic positions in the region.
The State Department said the previous distribution of foreign military financing did “not align with the administration’s prioritization of” the Western Hemisphere. Spending the money in South America will help recipients “combat narcoterrorism in our backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal” and “prevent adversaries from establishing strategic footholds in our hemisphere,” the department explained.
How did the South American recipients align with Trump?
Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, all four recipients have taken steps aligning themselves more closely with his administration’s priorities.
Panama withdrew from China’s Belt and Road Initiative and expanded security cooperation with Washington, though President Jose Raul Mulino pushed back on Trump’s suggestion that the US should retake direct control of the Panama Canal.
Mulino’s government has scrapped contracts with Hong Kong-based firm CK Hutchison Holdings, which Washington cited as evidence of a slow Chinese takeover of critical ports in Peru. The company owned by billionaire Li Ka-shing’s family is seeking $1.5 billion in damages.
Ecuador has signed a trade agreement with the US, lowering trade barriers and making other concessions to American exporters. President Daniel Noboa has also expanded counter-narcotics cooperation with Washington, tacitly endorsing Trump’s controversial tactics that involve airstrikes on boats in international waters that the Pentagon deems suspicious.
Noboa’s proposal to once again allow foreign military bases in Ecuador was rejected by voters last year.
Peru has joined Trump’s signature Shield of the Americas initiative under new President Keiko Fujimori, the daughter and political heir to dictator Alberto Fujimori, and otherwise expanding security cooperation with Washington.
Colombia too took a right-wing turn and realigned with Washington this year, after controversial President Abelardo de la Espriella came to power.
The millionaire nicknamed El Tigre (The Tiger) owns a personal luxury brand and used to represent drug traffickers as a lawyer. He has pledged to be tough on organized crime as president, including by resuming fumigation of coca with herbicides.
How is the ‘Donroe Doctrine’ being enforced?
The Trump administration has also used military and economic pressure elsewhere in the Western Hemisphere.
In January, US forces abducted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, and brought them to the US to face federal “narco-terrorism” charges. Trump subsequently said Washington would temporarily “run” Venezuela and tap its vast oil reserves.
During his first term from 2017 to 2021, Trump recognized opposition politician Juan Guaido as Venezuela’s interim president and supported his bid to replace Maduro.
Washington also tightened its trade blockade of Cuba this year, cutting off Venezuelan oil supplies and threatening retaliation against countries providing fuel to the island nation. The resulting fuel shortage has contributed to prolonged blackouts and a severe energy crisis.
Trump intervened directly in Honduras’ 2025 presidential race by publicly endorsing conservative candidate Nasry Asfura. He also pardoned former President Juan Orlando Hernandez, a fellow member of Asfura’s National Party who had been convicted in the US on drug trafficking charges.
In Colombia, former President Gustavo Petro alleged that the election won by de la Espriella had been digitally manipulated from abroad, pointing to alleged Israeli involvement and criticizing US interference in the campaign. Colombian electoral authorities rejected his fraud claims.
How is the ‘Donroe Doctrine’ different from the Monroe Doctrine?
US President James Monroe declared the Western Hemisphere off limits for European great powers in 1823.
While he framed his policy as anti-colonialist, in practice it prevented any military threat to the US homeland from emerging in South America and ensured preferential treatment of US businesses, particularly their access to natural resources, from bananas grown in Guatemala to copper mined in Chile.
US hegemony manifested during the 20th century in the so-called ‘dirty war’ against left-leaning political projects in South America. Washington supported right-wing dictatorships across the continent as long as they pledged to oppose Communism.
Since the end of the Cold War, Washington has defended its interests in South America under the guise of promoting human rights and democracy and dismantling narcotraffic, with the messaging shifting depending on which of the two US parties was holding the presidency.
Trump’s version distinguishes itself in its blatant approach rather than essence.

articles.title: Further US sanctions would complicate Ukraine peace efforts – Kremlin
articles.body:
Further US sanctions would complicate Ukraine peace efforts – Kremlin
Additional US sanctions against Russia would make it more difficult to reach a settlement of the Ukraine conflict, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
The US House of Representatives passed the legislation on Wednesday, following Senate approval last month, sending it to President Donald Trump for his signature. The bill allows Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
Commenting on the measure on Thursday, Peskov described it as an “unfriendly” move and said that Moscow was closely following its progress.
“Of course, the introduction of any additional sanctions by the US will definitely complicate efforts to find a peaceful settlement in Ukraine,” he told reporters.
The legislation, named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, had remained stalled for months as Trump pursued diplomatic efforts to settle the conflict. Graham, a vocal supporter of Kiev, had championed tougher sanctions against Russia.
US-mediated efforts to resolve the conflict largely paused after Trump launched a war against Iran in late February. Diplomatic contacts resumed earlier this month, when White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kiev.
The bill also targets Russia’s energy and defense sectors and its so-called “shadow fleet” of tankers allegedly used to evade sanctions. Its tariff provisions target major buyers of Russian energy, including China and India.
New Delhi said on Thursday that it was monitoring developments and would take “all necessary measures” to protect its economic interests and energy security. India has also warned the US that tariffs imposed over purchases of Russian oil could affect bilateral ties.
The measure faced opposition from many House Democrats, who argued that it could raise costs for Americans. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said that the legislation could give the president “unfettered authority” to impose tariffs.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected Western sanctions as illegal and ineffective. President Vladimir Putin has said that Russia has adapted its economy to mitigate their impact despite tens of thousands of restrictive measures imposed on the country.

articles.title: Fire temporarily shuts part of Slovak ammunition plant amid plans to triple capacity
articles.body:
ZVS Holding evacuated its ammunition factory in Snina, a town in eastern Slovakia, on 16 September after a fire broke out on the roof of a production building. Work stopped temporarily in the affected section, but nobody was injured, Militarnyi reported.
The Snina plant has an annual capacity of roughly 100,000 shells and plans to triple it, Noviny reported. The blaze briefly disrupted part of a facility under expansion for Europe’s ammunition buildup, although co-owner CSG expects no impact on customer deliveries. Authorities across Europe are investigating suspected Russian sabotage against defense companies, but no evidence links the Snina fire to that campaign.
ZVS Holding is owned equally by the Slovak state and the Czech defense conglomerate Czechoslovak Group (CSG). It makes 155 mm artillery shells, 120 mm tank rounds, and 30/35 mm cannon ammunition.
In December 2025, ZVS signed a seven-year framework agreement with Slovakia’s Defense Ministry to supply EU states. Purchases under the agreement may be financed through the bloc’s SAFE defense-loan program. Its Euro 58 billion ceiling represents the maximum possible value of future orders, not guaranteed purchases.
Firefighters brought the blaze under control during the afternoon. As thick black smoke rose over Snina, town officials advised nearby residents to limit time outdoors, close windows and doors, and switch off ventilation systems drawing in outside air.
Slovak Defense Minister Robert Kaliňák said the fire had not reached the plant’s production equipment and that the affected part of the building was not being used for manufacturing at the time. That section makes metal projectiles, he said.
Kaliňák said welding during the renovation may have sparked the fire, but stressed that investigators had not established the cause.
CSG said the fire started during roof repairs conducted by an external contractor. The company said the damage and cause still had to be assessed, but it did not expect the incident to affect customer deliveries, STVR reported.
Why sabotage fears shadow Europe’s arms plants
The Snina blaze was at least the fourth fire or explosion at a European ammunition facility since 10 August, after two fires struck a Bulgarian company and an explosion hit an Italian factory. No common cause has been established.
Preliminary findings pointed away from outside interference in the first Bulgarian fire. No evidence of sabotage, however, was reported after the Italian blast, and only the second Bulgarian fire remains under investigation for possible sabotage.
Czech authorities are examining a possible Russian trail behind an arson attack on a factory making drones and thermal optics for Ukraine.
Estonia has also probed suspected arson at a military-robot maker after courts documented earlier attacks directed by Russian military intelligence.

articles.title: At least 10 killed, 71 injured in Russian strikes across Ukraine over past day as Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa oblasts bear brunt of attacks
articles.body:
At least 10 killed, 75 injured in Russian strikes across Ukraine over past day as Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa oblasts bear brunt of attacks
Editor's note: This story was updated with revised figures for those injured in Kyiv in the overnight attack on Sept. 17.
At least 10 people were killed and 75 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, according to Ukrainian authorities.
The attack comes as the U.S. government backed sweeping legislation that would allow tariffs of up to 100% to be imposed on countries that purchase Russian oil and gas.
Russia launched a large-scale overnight attack on Ukrainian cities, using ballistic and cruise missiles, Shahed-type one-way attack drones, and Oniks anti-ship missiles.
The main targets of the Russian attack were the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Odesa oblasts, according to Ukraine's Air Force. Ukrainian forces shot down or suppressed with electronic warfare 124 of 157 Russian drones of various types, as well as seven of 10 low-cost "Banderol" cruise missiles, the Air Force said.
Russian missile and drone strikes were recorded at 36 locations across Ukraine, while drone debris was reported at five additional locations, according to the Air Force.
In Kyiv, 20 people, including two children, were injured in a series of overnight Russian drone and missile attacks, Mayor Vitali Klitshchko said.
In Donetsk Oblast, two people were killed and five others injured in Russian attacks, according to Governor Vadym Filashkin.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, five people were killed and seven injured when a Russian drone struck a civilian commuter bus in the Nikopol area, according to local authorities.
In Kherson Oblast, one person was killed and 14 others injured in a series of Russian drone, missile and air strikes targeting the city of Kherson and surrounding settlements, local authorities said.
In Kirovohrad Oblast, Russian strikes hit the center of Kropyvnytskyi, injuring at least four people, according to local authorities.
In Sumy Oblast, one man was killed in a Russian air strike, while 14 others, including two children, were injured in other Russian attacks, the local military administration said.
In Odesa Oblast, one person was killed in a Russian strike on Sept. 16, while six others were injured in overnight attacks, Governor Serhii Lysak said.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, five people were injured in Russian attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia and surrounding areas, according to local authorities.

articles.title: Taiwan military tests Land Sword II missile
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The military test-fired its domestically developed Land Sword II air defense missile Thursday as part of a multi-day joint precision weapons exercise at Jiupeng Military Base in Pingtung County.
The exercise also featured the Hsiung Sheng missile and Chien Hsiang loitering munition system, following Wednesday's opening phase, which included Patriot missile launches and other major weapons systems, per Liberty Times. The live-fire tests were designed to assess the military's long-range strike capabilities, air defense response, and overall combat readiness.
The Hsiung Sheng was launched first, followed by the Chien Hsiang and the Land Sword II, a land-based variant of the air-to-air Sky Sword II. The Land Sword II launch demonstrated the air defense forces' mobility and interception capabilities.
President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) is scheduled to visit the Jiupeng base Friday to inspect the exercise, Liberty Times reported. The demonstration is expected to include live-fire tests of Tien Kung III, Hsiung Feng III, and Hsiung Feng II missiles, HIMARS multiple rocket launchers, Maverick missiles, loitering munitions, Altius-600M systems, and attack drones.

articles.title: Evening news wrap: Tata Trusts-Chandrasekaran row, Russia hits out at US sanctions bill, Putin’s birthday message to PM Modi & more
articles.body:
A major governance dispute has emerged at Tata Sons after Tata Trusts called N Chandrasekaran’s reappointment as chairman for another five-year term “illegal”. The Trusts said the resolution was a “legal nullity” because nominee director Noel N Tata voted against it.
The Kremlin has described the US House of Representatives’ passage of a sweeping Russia sanctions bill as an “unfriendly” action, warning that tougher US sanctions could complicate diplomatic efforts to secure a peace deal and resolve the ongoing Ukraine conflict.
Russian president Vladimir Putin congratulated Prime Minister Narendra Modi on his 76th birthday, praising his role in strengthening the “special and privileged” strategic partnership between India and Russia. Putin also thanked Modi for the warm welcome and hospitality during his recent New Delhi visit.
The Supreme Court directed Tamil Nadu to comply with its order to identify land for Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas in every district, while urging dialogue with the Centre. The bench questioned the state’s opposition to the schools’ three-language policy, including Hindi.
A video by 2021-batch IPS officer Bushra Bano about her UPSC journey and AMU’s Residential Coaching Academy drew criticism on social media. She used expressions including “Assalamualaikum”, “Inshallah” and “Jazakallah” before being transferred as deputy commandant.
Here are your top stories of the day:
Tata trusts challenge Chandrasekaran reappointment, calling it ‘illegal’
A fresh governance dispute has emerged at Tata Sons after Tata Trusts said the board’s decision to give N Chandrasekaran another five-year term was a “legal nullity”, arguing that the required Trust nominee support was absent. Tata Trusts said Chandrasekaran’s earlier decision not to seek another term as Tata Sons chairman had already been accepted and had “attained finality”. The Trusts said he communicated the decision to the Tata Sons board on August 12. The dispute comes alongside the board’s decision to proceed with a potential Tata Sons listing after the RBI rejected its bid to surrender its core investment company registration. Read full story.
Russia warns US sanctions bill could complicate Ukraine peace efforts
The Kremlin has described the US House of Representatives’ passage of a sweeping Russia sanctions bill as an “unfriendly” action and warned that further sanctions could make efforts to reach a Ukraine peace settlement more difficult. The comments come as the US House passed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by 262-159. The legislation would allow sanctions on Russia and tariffs of up to 100% on major purchasers of Russian oil or gas, with implications for countries including India and China.
Putin praises Modi’s role in strengthening India-Russia ties
Russian President Vladimir Putin has wished Prime Minister Narendra Modi on his 76th birthday and credited him with strengthening the “special and privileged” strategic partnership between the two countries. Putin also referred to his recent visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit, describing the talks with PM Modi as “substantive, frank, and productive”, saying the discussions demonstrated the PM's “extraordinary political wisdom and foresight”. Read full story.
Supreme Court asks Tamil Nadu to identify land for Navodaya schools
The Supreme Court has given Tamil Nadu three more months to identify suitable land in every district for Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas, while asking the state and Centre to continue discussions over the schools’ language policy. The state has opposed the three-language approach followed by Navodaya schools, which includes Hindi, citing Tamil Nadu’s existing two-language policy. Justice BV Nagarathna said, “You have to change your mindset, it can’t be that Hindi will not be taught in the soil of Tamil Nadu.
” The bench also urged cooperative federalism, saying people in Chennai should not alienate those in Delhi. Read full story.
IPS officer Bushra Bano transferred after UPSC video draws criticism
A video by Bengal IPS officer Bushra Bano about her UPSC preparation drew criticism on social media after she used expressions including “Assalamualaikum”, “Inshallah” and “Jazakallah”. In the September 13 video, Bano spoke about AMU’s Residential Coaching Academy and its role in her preparation. She was later transferred from additional SP of Kharagpur to deputy commandant of the state armed police, though the transfer order did not cite the video or criticism. Read full story.

articles.title: Carney Says Canada and E.U. 'Are Not Fair Weather Allies' as Trump Threatens Europe Over 'Hostile Act'
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday welcomed the prospect of Canada becoming an “associate member” of the E.U., just hours after U.S. President Donald Trump dismissed the proposal as “laughable.”
Addressing the European Parliament as a guest of honor in Strasbourg, France, Carney insisted “Europe and Canada are stronger together” and said “Canada and the European Union can anchor our ground to hold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive.”
Carney’s pivot toward Europe comes as he seeks to establish stronger international ties and curtail Canada’s reliance on the American market amid an all-out trade war. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect last week, matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. after negotiations collapsed last month. Trump’s repeated threats against Canadian sovereignty and calls to make it the “51st state” have added to the months-long tension.
While Carney did not directly mention Trump or his Administration while addressing European lawmakers, he appeared to make nods to the current volatility of Canada-U.S. relations and condemned economic coercions. Speaking about the "current geopolitical rupture," he said a "new dimension was needed.”
“Economic integration is now being weaponized, tariffs being used to exert pressure,” he said. “Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited.”
Championing the burgeoning E.U. alliance, Carney focused on what he said were shared values between Canada and the bloc, insisting: "We are not fair-weather allies. We believe that our prosperity grows when it is shared."
“I'm not proposing a third bloc in order to become a 'great power' rival, only with better manners,” Carney continued. “We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”
Carney, who began his speech in French—one of Canada’s official languages—before continuing in English, with splatterings of German, welcomed how European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen had on Wednesday opened the door for Canada becoming an “associate member” of the 27-member bloc.
When speaking about forging closer ties with the E.U., Carney referenced seeking strategic autonomy through “deep co-operation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defense industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space and payments.” He insisted Canada and Europe must not be dependent on “individual nations or individual companies” as this “creates vulnerabilities, particularly when supposedly global companies prove national in the breach.”
He also hinted at a potential freedom of movement between the E.U. and Canada that would allow “youth to work, study, and live where they want, on either side of the Atlantic.”
Carney’s passionate advocacy for the deepening of ties with the E.U.—a move he says Canadians have shown they’re in support of—came after Trump lambasted the idea of a new European dawn for Canada.
Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Trump called the proposal “laughable” and threatened economic punishments if the E.U. moves forward with von der Leyen’s plan.
"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump said en route to an event in North Carolina. "If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”
In response to Trump’s remarks, a European Commission spokesperson told TIME: “As president von der Leyen made clear [on Wednesday], the proposed strengthening of our partnership with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”
Carney welcomes new alliances on visit to Europe
Carney's speech to the European Parliament came on the final day of his stay in Europe, where he sought to cement and deepen Canada’s international relationships.
The E.U. is Canada’s second-largest global trading partner for goods and services, with bilateral trade worth approximately C$178.6 billion in 2025.
The Canadian leader also traveled to Liverpool, England, to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The pair attended a football game and watched Everton—the team they both support—secure a victory against the Wolverhampton Wanderers.
"The leaders began by underscoring the close co-operation between the U.K. and Canada and emphasized the importance of building similar close ties with European partners, particularly on trade and defence,” a Downing Street spokeswoman told TIME.
Ahead of the meeting, Burnham called Carney a “great progressive leader” with whom the U.K. shares “so many values, but also with whom we have a shared opportunity on defense co-operation, on trade” and AI.
Canada applies to join U.K.-led military coalition
Following Burnham and Carney's meeting, it was announced that Canada has applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military coalition.
The force, formally launched in 2014, consists of 10 North Atlantic NATO member states that deliver rapid response and security operations.
“Prime Minister Carney announced that Canada has formally applied to join the Joint Expeditionary Force and welcomed the U.K.’s support for Canada’s participation in this important initiative,” Carney’s office said in a statement.
Canada, already a NATO member, is seeking to diversify its defense dependency from the U.S. with new partnerships across the Atlantic.
In February, Canada became the first non-European country to participate in the "Security action for Europe” (SAFE) instrument, which provides up to €150 billion in low-interest loans to help member states purchase military and defense equipment.
What happens next as Canada seeks "associate" membership with the E.U.?
Following von der Leyen’s proposal, a European Commission spokesperson told TIME that the executive cabinet will work “in close coordination with [its] member states and the European Parliament” to “create a new form of partnership that has not existed until now–building the closest imaginable form of association with a partner outside Europe.”
The proposed alliance is set to include deeper economic ties, a technology alliance, greater integration of defense industrial bases, and efforts to make the Arctic a flagship joint project. It could also expand cooperation on energy, critical minerals and batteries, as well as AI, quantum technology, cybersecurity, and economic security.
The E.U.-Canada summit set to take place in Montreal in late October will “provide the first meaningful opportunity to discuss these issues further,” the spokesperson told TIME.
The proposal has been welcomed by many European lawmakers across the bloc.
Member of the European Parliament (MEP) for Spain Javier Moreno Sánchez, who also serves as chair of the parliament’s delegation for relations with Canada, told TIME the decision to bring Canada in as an “associate member” was “politically and symbolically significant,” but warned it “must now be followed by concrete actions.”
Irish MEP Barry Andrews told TIME that the announcement is a clear “win-win for both sides,” adding that “in an ever more insecure world, truly democratic countries must come together and stand up to Trump, [Chinese President] Xi Jinping, and [Russian President Vladimir] Putin.”
Germany, the E.U.’s largest economy, also embraced the move, with government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius saying Berlin “welcomes the initiative for a particularly close partnership with Canada.”
The E.U., much like Canada, is seeking new partnerships amid a weakening alliance with the U.S. under Trump, following disputes over tariff threats, his lashing out at the NATO alliance, and his push to annex Greenland.
Espen Barth Eide, Norway’s Foreign Affairs Minister, told TIME the world is "living through the most serious security situation since the Second World War.”
“At a time like this, it is welcome that the E.U. is strengthening cooperation on European security. We also welcome the E.U.’s efforts to involve Norway, the United Kingdom, Canada and Iceland. Such an approach strengthens European security,” he said.
Norway and Iceland are not members of the E.U., but both belong to the European Economic Area (EEA), giving them close economic ties to the bloc through trade and free movement—a model from which Canada could draw inspiration.
Elsewhere, the “associate” membership proposal faced backlash.
French MEP Manon Aubry, co-chair of The Left group, told TIME there was “a serious question of method,” arguing that “a decision of such magnitude cannot be made by the president of the European Commission alone.”

articles.title: UN finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UN mission finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran, and Tehran crimes against humanity
A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined US conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.
The Pentagon declined to comment on a report conducted by an outside organization.
"Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment," it said in a statement. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in response to the report that the UN Human Rights Council had "accomplished nothing for human rights," adding that Iran was the only party in the current conflict that had committed war crimes.
The Iranian permanent mission in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
U.S. officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
UN Fact-Finding missions are investigative, not judicial bodies, and therefore do not initiate any criminal cases.
Their findings, however, can be used in criminal investigations by national courts or international tribunals such as the International Criminal Court. States will discuss the findings of the report when it is presented to the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Monday.
MINAB SCHOOL STRIKE
The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.
According to the report, the US failure to update information in relation to the school, which was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval complex, in its targeting databases and to confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
"Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."
In June US President Donald Trump said that "nobody" purposefully attacked a girls' school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. Reuters news agency first reported that an initial internal US military investigation showed US forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran.
The Pentagon has since elevated the probe but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.
The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
U.S. Central Command said in a statement in March that U.S. forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
IRAN ABUSES
The UN mission probe found that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes the U.S. and Israel.
The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures which say 3,038 people were killed, and 25,000 people injured.
The government's response to the protests — including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty — marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

articles.title: Thousands are starving in occupied Oleshky. People have no food, no way out, and Russian forces bomb incoming aid
articles.body:
Oleshky, a Ukrainian city under Russian occupation in Kherson Oblast, is facing a severe humanitarian crisis, with more than 6,000 people, including around 200 children, potentially trapped there, according to Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets.
Civilians are going without food, drinking water, medicine, and other basic necessities while facing daily shelling and drone attacks, Lubinets said.
The crisis has become so desperate that some residents are trying to escape on their own without waiting for an organized evacuation, crossing mined fields because they see no other way out. They risk being killed by mines or Russian drones, but are attempting to leave because staying in Oleshky has become even more dangerous.
“People need to be saved,” Lubinets said, describing the city as a “death trap.”
Thousands remain trapped
Lubinets said his office has received 176 appeals concerning the humanitarian situation in the temporarily occupied territories of Kherson Oblast and has verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to safely leave the area.
He stressed that these are only people his office has managed to identify. Based on the population of Oleshky and the surrounding area, more than 6,000 people may still remain there, including around 200 children, he said.
The civilians remaining in the city are effectively in a “gray zone,” according to Lubinets. They face daily shelling and drone attacks while lacking food, drinking water, medicine, and other essential assistance.
“The stories make your blood run cold. And so there is only one task — to get our people out of this deadly danger,” Lubinets said.
“There is real hunger there”
Other reporting indicates that the shortages have persisted for months. According to Kherson Regional Military Administration head Oleksandr Prokudin, food deliveries to Oleshky have almost completely stopped, while Russian forces prevent residents from evacuating.
Natalia Soboleva, an Odesa volunteer who tracks the situation in Oleshky, told Espreso that residents are gathering grass and searching through destroyed basements for food.
“There is hunger there, real hunger,” she said.
The blockade has also affected humanitarian efforts. Soboleva said Russian forces attacked humanitarian vehicles attempting to bring food and water into the city. During the latest reported attempt on 1 September, Russian troops shelled four volunteer vehicles.
The crisis in Oleshky has been independently documented by international organizations and media. The UN, Human Rights Watch and the OSCE have all reported severe shortages of food and medical care, dangerous conditions for civilians, and restrictions on humanitarian aid and evacuation.
International monitors confirm Russia’s blockade of occupied Oleshky, where the living starve and the dead go unburied
Russia has not confirmed evacuation, so civilians risk mines to escape
The ombudsman said some people are now trying to leave independently. They are crossing mined areas despite the risk of being killed by a mine or targeted by a drone because they do not see another way to escape.
This desperation has also been documented by Human Rights Watch, which said there is no organized evacuation route from Oleshky and that people attempting to leave face Russian military checkpoints and a dangerous journey through occupied territory.
Lubinets said Ukraine has been pressing for an organized humanitarian evacuation.
Ukraine and Russia had previously reached agreements and established clear procedures for such a mission, he said. Lubinets also secured the International Committee of the Red Cross’ readiness to participate within its mandate.
Ukraine prepared a list of people for evacuation and coordinated with its Security and Defense Forces to establish a ceasefire during the humanitarian mission.
But Russia has not confirmed its readiness to carry out the evacuation, according to Lubinets.
Mined in, starved out, hunted from above—life in the towns Russia demands at the peace table
Months ago, he said, he informed international organizations, including the United Nations and the ICRC headquarters in Geneva, about the critical situation and called for assistance to prevent mass deaths.
Lubinets said his office continues to collect and verify information and coordinate with the ICRC, international organizations and Ukrainian authorities. It is also continuing to press Russia for an urgent evacuation of civilians remaining in Oleshky.
The situation is difficult to independently verify because Oleshky is under Russian occupation and access to the city is severely restricted. But reports of the humanitarian crisis have been corroborated by the UN, Human Rights Watch, the OSCE and other international organizations, as well as Ukrainian and international media.
