articles.title: Russia’s International Youth Festival reportedly drew representatives from 191 countries. Foreign attendees got unrestricted internet access. Russian attendees did not.
articles.body:
Russia’s International Youth Festival reportedly drew representatives from 191 countries. Foreign attendees got unrestricted internet access. Russian attendees did not.
The International Youth Festival has wrapped up in Yekaterinburg after running from September 11 to 17. Rosmolodezh, the festival’s organizer, had said 10,000 people would attend: 5,000 from Russia and another 5,000 from other countries. Representatives from 191 countries reportedly took part — nearly the entire world. The United Nations has 193 member states.
The festival featured: Dima Bilan, Vanya Dmitrienko, Egor Kreed, and Zveri, as well as Natalia Oreiro and Steven Seagal — foreign celebrities with Russian passports. There were also exhibitions about restored churches in the Donbas and neo-Nazism in the 21st century. And dancing in kokoshniks. And a five-meter-long kulebyaka. And merchandise bearing quotes from Putin.
But the festival’s biggest surprise was that Russian and foreign attendees received different levels of internet access. Three Wi-Fi networks were available at Yekaterinburg Expo, where the festival was held: a restricted network for Russians, an unrestricted network for foreigners, and a separate network for speakers and organizers whose settings are unknown. Attendees could connect using the personal number on their badge, and the system automatically barred Russian participants from joining the unrestricted network for foreigners.
Foreigners also received SIM cards that provided access to blocked services, apparently so they could use the internet without restrictions both at the festival venue and elsewhere. “The SIM cards issued to foreign delegates do indeed allow them to access the services they normally use abroad,” the festival hotline told Agentstvo.
Sergey Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff of Russia’s Presidential Administration, said foreign guests received unrestricted internet access so they could promote the festival to audiences in other countries. “It’s good when Russians talk about Russia. But there’s much more trust when people in those countries hear about Russia from their own peers. That changes the attitudes of the friends they share it with and their followers,” he said.
What could the foreign guests tell their friends and followers? For example, that a war between Russia and Europe would be very short. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said as much at the festival: “We have said more than once that we have no intention of attacking Europe. But if Europe, which talks every day about preparing for war against Russia, attacks Russia, that will be an entirely different war, and it will be very short.”
Or that Alabuga Polytech is an excellent educational project. Maxim Oreshkin, deputy chief of staff of the Presidential Administration, said it was. The college in Tatarstan became known for having students assemble Iranian Shahed-type drones, which Russia uses to attack Ukraine. According to an investigation by the outlet Protokol, Alabuga students struggled to balance work and study, worked overtime without extra pay, and feared refusing to assemble drones because they feared being expelled and having to pay compensation to the college.

articles.title: Russia’s elections weren’t always this dishonest. Here’s how the system broke down and why voting can still expose fraud.
articles.body:
Russia’s elections weren’t always this dishonest. Here’s how the system broke down and why voting can still expose fraud.
Russians will vote for members of the State Duma from September 18 to 20. The authorities are counting on a solid — though not triumphant — victory; the opposition is both uniting and quarreling as it searches for the best protest-voting strategy; and many potential voters are growing more skeptical about the whole idea of showing up at a polling station or using the remote electronic voting system, since the results will be “faked” anyway. How reasonable is that view? Are elections in Russia really illegitimate from the outset? Which ones were the most dishonest? And how do you find the motivation to take part when you know everything has already been decided? Meduza put these and other questions about electoral fraud to a veteran researcher of Russian elections. (We cannot disclose the expert’s name for security reasons, but we have full confidence in his expertise.)
How do we know that elections in Russia are illegitimate?
If you take legitimacy to mean compliance with the law, then monitoring at practically every major election shows the problem is systemic. And the departures from the rules happen at all sorts of levels — from the rooms where election commissions work all the way up to federal law.
Public monitoring projects — such as the “Map of Violations” run by the Golos movement — usually document violations mainly at the precinct commissions. Observers, meanwhile, show that the higher-level commissions have no interest in following the law either. And the lawyers who challenge violations regularly find problems in the regulations themselves. The way the system responds tells you what its priorities and goals are.
Ideally, commission rulings and legislation would address the problems identified. Instead, they almost always just create new ones.
- In recent years, for example, Russia abolished the role of election commission members with advisory voting rights. That was a blow to election monitoring: you can no longer show up at a polling station without drawing the attention of the local administration well in advance (and territorial commissions are housed in administration buildings in nearly 100% of cases).
- Multiday voting has also made observation far harder.
- Video feeds that once allowed the public to monitor activity at polling stations have been unavailable since 2021.
The authorities’ approach essentially boils down to this: we’ll ban everything and make it physically impossible to monitor the elections. Rather than saying: We have nothing to hide. Let anyone observe, and keep voting to a single day.
How the system responds to violations is the single best measure of legitimacy. As a rule, investigative agencies forward criminal complaints to the election commissions, and the commissions simply take the word of the very people the observer is accusing.
What matters is precisely how the system closes itself off in response to violations. In 2018, during the gubernatorial election in Primorye, observers discovered that 13 tally sheets — the official precinct results documents that led the Central Election Commission to recommend annulling the results — had not in fact been lost in a fire, as the official account claimed, but had been entered into the Vybory state automated system. Anyone could see on the commission’s website that the tally sheets existed; they had simply been hidden. It became obvious that the commission was lying. And the response? That same day, the commission’s website removed the ability to view the history of tally sheets entered into the system.
There is statistical evidence of fraud as well. Observers with the volunteer project Peresmotr drew attention to a provision of Federal Law No. 67 under which an election must be declared invalid if it was invalid at precincts accounting for at least 25% of the voters who cast ballots. Checking for fraud using recordings of the official video broadcast of the 2021 State Duma elections (Meduza covered the analysis of that footage in detail), the volunteers confirmed that the violations affected more than 25% of voters — meaning the elections should have been declared invalid. That, of course, did not happen, because election commissions at every level don’t follow the law.
Territorial commissions often go further, helping people committing violations in the precincts by ignoring observers’ reports. In effect, the system of election commissions operates as one large criminal organization.
Electoral statistics add to what observers see. Spikes at round numbers in turnout or results (you can read more about these anomalies in this Meduza piece) show that, at every federal election, the results are fabricated as if by calculator. The most recent Russian presidential election was no exception.
Has Russia ever counted votes honestly?
Elections were not always as dishonest as they have been in the last few electoral cycles. The slide to today’s situation was gradual. As an article on the Golos website points out, for instance, the results of the 2000 election were counted relatively honestly. But things got worse year by year. By 2004, observers were already documenting the “calculator” fabrication described above, and from 2007 onward, vote distributions took on a comet-like shape with a pronounced tail indicating ballot stuffing.
Even now, results are sometimes counted without heavy fraud. Five years ago in the Khabarovsk region, for example, United Russia took a modest 25% — a figure close to its real level of support. Assessing the 2018 elections, experts writing for Meduza identified as many as 12 relatively honest regions.
It’s worth remembering that counting the votes takes only a few hours, while an election campaign lasts months. So this is entirely possible: an honest count but a dishonest, predetermined result.
Observers at the polling stations see this most clearly. They make fraud harder, but they often note that a majority of voters really do vote for Putin. A Putin who has been spared any real competitors, since those were kept off the ballot on contrived grounds. When election commissions and courts decide who will be on the ballot, it’s important to remember that dishonest elections begin at exactly that stage, which is invisible to voters on election day.
Russians lost real elections a long ago. But you’ve still got a choice. If you live outside Russia, please donate to Meduza — for yourself or for those who remain inside the country and want to read independent news.
Is it possible to say which elections were the most dishonest?
For a long time it was Dmitry Medvedev’s election, with its enormous tail of ballot stuffing and plenty of other evidence pointing to “faked” results. The vote on the constitutional amendments later broke that record. Election analyst Sergey Shpilkin estimated that about 20 million “yes” votes were added. But even the “voting on tree stumps” — a nickname earned when ballot boxes were set up outdoors on stumps — was eclipsed by Putin’s 2024 election, with an anomalous 22 million excess votes cast for him. So far that’s the record.
My guess is that we could set a new record this year. Removing Yabloko — a party that, according to pollsters, was on track for a double-digit result — from the ballot deprives millions of people of their preferred choice.
Which kinds of fraud are the most common? Ballot stuffing? Remote voting? Something else?
The people committing the fraud seem to have learned the saying about not putting all your eggs in one basket. There’s no single method. Often several techniques are used at a single election. In the Primorye vote mentioned above, three types of fraud were used at once: paper tally sheets were rewritten, the results of tally sheets already entered were hidden, and results were changed after they had been entered into the Vybory system.
Today the whole toolkit is in use: ballot stuffing during home visits, ballot stuffing into the sealed bags that hold votes overnight, supervised voting through the online system, precinct tallies faked by several different methods, those tallies rewritten at territorial election commissions, and tallies deleted from Vybory, the state election database. The list goes on.
If you had to pick just one, it’s ballot stuffing, of course. And it has gotten smarter. Three-day voting is far more convenient for those committing fraud: ballots can be stuffed into a tamper-evident bag overnight, and then observers can be kept from finding out. If the observer pushes back and insists on documenting the violation, people give false testimony against them, and the court removes them, supposedly for interfering with the commission’s work.
Is it possible for Russians to fight electoral fraud at all, or is it totally pointless?
You can always fight. It will not be very effective, which makes the work of election observers all the more heroic. But be prepared: it is precisely in fighting the people who falsify results that you come to understand just how bad Russia’s elections have become. Dealing with investigative agencies, the courts, and the election commissions above the one committing the fraud, you will most likely see that not one of them has any interest in upholding the law.
When you learn that through personal experience, it strengthens your convictions. In any case, in my view, standing by while our country’s electoral system is destroyed is clearly not an option.
Is there any doubt that the 2026 elections will be stolen from Russians?
Sadly, almost none. The theft began several months ago, when the authorities started removing candidates they considered undesirable from the race, especially those from the pro-peace Yabloko party. And these violations are happening right now; we see them in the news every day. So the theft is already underway. And remember the “innovations” listed above that make life easier for those committing fraud — from three-day voting and the closing off of video recordings from polling stations to the expansion of early voting and remote electronic voting.
What’s the point of participating in an election that will be stolen?
The election will be stolen — but not your vote. Casting that vote gives you a way to challenge the crooks at polling stations and tell people around you about violations. If, for example, you take your ballot away instead of casting it and later see that your precinct’s tally does not account for it, you have effectively uncovered fraud.
Elections still create a space for people in Russia to talk about something that matters to them. And because not all votes are stolen, we can still get at least local violations corrected.
One important point: the laws still partly work. When observers take on the election commissions, they are still relying on the rules as they exist. And commissions are required to respond to such complaints (as a rule, they even meet the procedural deadlines!). So there is, at a minimum, a point in shining a light on the cheating.
Here’s an example. The Central Election Commission’s ruling on video surveillance states that video must be provided on request if an observer who was present at the count has filed a complaint against the precinct commission. Yes, they will refuse requests from people who don’t know this. But if you filed a complaint, were present at the count, filled out the application correctly, and sent it to your regional commission, the chances of a refusal are already very small. With proper preparation, you can break through that wall of automatic refusals and either obtain evidence of fraud or at least expose the election-commission establishment’s hypocrisy.
Another reason to take part is that the more authorities’ opponents vote, the harder it is to falsify the results. If you showed up on Sunday and voted, your vote is harder to fake than if you had stayed home. Falsification is a complicated process, and it always leaves traces.
Video from polling stations is now available to practically no one, but recordings of these crimes will be stored on servers for a full year. Candidates’ observers can file complaints en masse (to obtain the clips showing violations) and then publish either the footage or the refusals to hand it over.
What’s the better way to vote to prevent fraud: in person or online?
The best option is in person, on Sunday evening, at the precinct where you are also serving as an observer. But not everyone is able to observe, so my advice is a paper ballot. It’s more reliable. Remote electronic voting was introduced this year mainly in regions where the level of fraud is below average, so the probability of your vote being stolen online is most likely higher than at a polling station.
One more thing: an important change in 2026 is that even if you signed up for remote electronic voting and didn’t manage to withdraw that application through the Gosuslugi state services portal, you can still vote at your precinct. If you were forced to register for online voting, it’s still better to go to the precinct. The commission will have to check that you did not receive an electronic ballot, strike you from the remote voting list, and add you to a supplementary list at the precinct. We don’t know, though, whether every commission in all 32 regions covered by federal remote electronic voting will be equipped with computers connected to the system.

articles.title: Alleged Trickbot hacker wanted by Germany served as adviser to deputy chair of Russia’s State Duma
articles.body:
Vitaly Kovalev, who is wanted by German authorities as the alleged founder and leader of Trickbot, one of the largest cybercriminal groups in the world, worked as an adviser to Russian State Duma Deputy Speaker Vladislav Davankov and ran for the State Duma on the New People party’s ticket. The GangExposed project first drew attention to the connection between Kovalev and Davankov.
Davankov himself wrote in August 2025 that Kovalev had been his adviser for “more than a year,” describing him as a supporter of New People, an entrepreneur, and a med tech investor. Together they visited the longevity laboratory at Volgograd State Medical University (VolgSMU), and Kovalev, according to Davankov, was tasked with promoting the university’s products in the region. Davankov’s post was also shared by VolgSMU’s official channel.
Kovalev was nominated to run for the State Duma with New People. However, when the party’s federal list was certified on July 10, the state-controlled Vedomosti newspaper reported that Kovalev had been removed from regional group No. 18, which included Kalmykia and the Astrakhan and Volgograd regions. Kovalev’s is no longer among the 298 names on the list that was ultimately registered by the Central Election Commission.
Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) is seeking Vitaly Nikolayevich Kovalev, born June 23, 1988. German investigators believe that under the aliases Stern and Ben, he founded and led the Trickbot hacker group. His wanted notice also lists other aliases: Grave, Vincent, Bentley, Bergen, and Alex Konor. The BKA believes Kovalev is in Russia.
According to the BKA, Trickbot had been operating since at least 2016 and, at various points, boasted more than 100 members, who used its infrastructure for spreading malware of the same name, as well as the Bazarloader, SystemBC, IcedID, Ryuk, Conti, and Diavol tools. The group has infected hundreds of thousands of computer systems worldwide, earning hundreds of millions of euros from its criminal activity. Its victims have included hospitals, government agencies, companies, and private individuals.
In May 2025, German authorities obtained international arrest warrants for members of various cybercriminal groups as part of Operation Endgame. The BKA stated that international warrants had been issued for 20 suspects and that an Interpol Red Notice was also issued for Kovalev, obligating law enforcement agencies in other countries to locate him and, if possible, provisionally detain him pending an extradition decision.
In July 2026, the Council of the EU added Kovalev to its sanctions list over his involvement in cyberattacks. The document lists Kovalev’s full name, date of birth, and the aliases Bentley, Bergen, Alex Konor, Benny, Ben, and Stern. The EU describes Kovalev as a senior figure linked to the Trickbot group and Conti malware and holds him responsible for cyberattacks that caused significant economic damage.
Trickbot was used for initial access into computer systems, theft of banking and personal data, and the subsequent deployment of ransomware. The U.S. Department of Justice stated that Trickbot had infected millions of computers, including at hospitals, schools, and companies, and that its infrastructure was used to spread Conti.
Conti became one of the largest ransomware operations in history. According to the U.S. Department of Justice, it was used in more than a thousand attacks worldwide, and ransoms paid by victims exceeded $150 million. The FBI recorded at least 16 Conti attacks on U.S. medical and emergency networks, including ambulance services, police, and 911 dispatch centers. Worldwide, more than 400 organizations were affected.
Ransomware linked to Trickbot’s infrastructure caused especially severe damage to healthcare systems during the COVID-19 pandemic. Materials from a U.S. Senate hearing state that more than 200 attacks using Ryuk, which is closely tied to the Trickbot and Conti ecosystem, resulted in nearly $100 million in lost revenue for medical organizations and roughly $500 million in system recovery costs.

articles.title: India vows ‘determined’ response to US sanctions pressure
articles.body:
India vows ‘determined’ response to US sanctions pressure
India has said it remains “firmly committed” to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people, in response to the threat of steep new tariffs from the Russia sanctions bill that cleared the US Congress on Wednesday. 
“The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” the Indian Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Thursday. 
The new US bill mandates up to 100% additional trade tariffs on the top buyers of Russian oil. India is the second-largest buyer of Russian oil, after China. 
Russian crude accounted for 45% of Indian oil imports in August, at around 2.1 million barrels per day. New Delhi bought $40.8 billion of Russian crude in the financial year that ended in March, or about 30.3% of its total crude imports, according to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) think tank. 
The House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in a 262-159 vote on Wednesday, following the bill’s approval by the Senate last month. The legislation now goes to US President Donald Trump to be signed into law.
Our statement on passage of the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act in the US Congress
🔗 https://t.co/kD0Yg9sWbUpic.twitter.com/rSc21AqwEh
The Indian Foreign Ministry said the issue had been discussed at high levels in recent months with US officials, and that New Delhi had clearly conveyed the potential implications for both bilateral relations and the international energy market.
The Indian government will work closely with trade and industry bodies to deal with the implications, the Foreign Ministry said, adding New Delhi would continue to ensure energy security through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics.
The pressure on India to cut off Russian oil also comes amid the conflict in the Middle East, triggered by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, which have disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz and stoked energy prices.
The legislation does not automatically impose additional tariffs on Russian energy buyers, although it does give Trump the authority to impose extra duties on the top five importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas. India has held off on signing a trade deal with the US despite months of negotiations.
Analysts have said Trump could use the new tariff bill to pressure India to make unilateral trade concessions. The bill, named after late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, a known Russia hawk, also targets Russia’s energy and defense industries and vessels Washington claims are used to evade existing sanctions, while extending sanctions on Iran.

articles.title: China, India push back against US pressure over Russia sanctions
articles.body:
China and India on Thursday pushed back against a sweeping US sanctions and tariff bill targeting Russia, warning against measures that could disrupt trade ties and global energy markets.
The US House of Representatives approved the bill on Wednesday by a 262-159 vote, with dozens of Democrats joining Republicans. The measure now goes to US President Donald Trump for his signature.
The legislation targets senior Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, as well as oligarchs, state-owned companies and foreign businesses supporting Russia’s defence industry.
It also authorises the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries purchasing Russian oil and gas, including China and India.
“China carries out economic and trade cooperation with countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
Guo, however, said China’s “cooperation does not target any third party and it should not be disrupted under the coercion of any third party.”
“We always oppose long-arm jurisdiction that has no basis in international law or authority of UN Security Council,” he stressed.
Chinese and Russian bilateral trade has grown over the years, surging over $240 billion in 2024, and most of the trade is conducted in national currencies.
India
India, meanwhile, said it remained firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its people and would continue sourcing supplies from diverse sellers based on market dynamics.
New Delhi also said that it had warned Washington that any such new moves could impact ties between the two countries.
The Indian foreign ministry said that it had noted the passage of the bill, adding that New Delhi had raised the issue with various US interlocutors in recent months, and had "very clearly articulated" the potential implications for the bilateral relationship and the international energy market.
"The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests," it said in a statement.
The government would work closely with trade and industry bodies to deal with the implications of the legislation, it added.
India, the world's third-biggest oil importer, is among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, which is seen as helping Moscow replenish its budget since it launched its full-scale war with Ukraine in 2022 and was hit with sweeping Western sanctions.
New Delhi has repeatedly sought to resist pressure to scale back its oil trade with Russia, saying its large population and economy need secure, affordable and reliable energy supplies.

articles.title: UN mission finds 'reasonable grounds to believe US committed war crimes' in Iran
articles.body:
Ilayda Cakirtekin
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
- It also finds Iran's 'violent repression of 2025-2026 protests' marked by 'widespread use of lethal force resulting in mass killings, injuries, extensive arrests'
A UN fact-finding mission found on Thursday that the US committed war crimes during airstrikes on Iran, causing the death of civilians, injuries, and damage to civilian objects in Iran.
The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran issued a report, finding reasonable grounds to believe that the US committed war crimes "during a pair of airstrikes which killed at least 178 civilians, including women and children."
The mission noted that the war crimes included "launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects," during the US and Israeli attacks in February.
The cited attacks involved Tomahawk missile strikes on a primary school in Minab, which killed over 150 and another airstrike where Precision Strike Missiles dispersed clouds of tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area in Lamerd, killing 22 civilians.
"Civilians in Iran are caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own Government and the nation’s deadly conflict with the United States and Israel," the mission said.
The report also concluded that the Iranian government's "violent repression of the 2025-2026 protests marked an unprecedented escalation from past crackdowns, marked by the widespread use of lethal force resulting in mass killings and injuries, and extensive arrests."
It also criticized the government's imposition of a nationwide internet and communications blackout in January, during the height of protests.
The mission "urged Iran and the US to immediately cease all violations and crimes, provide full reparations to victims, and guarantee non-repetition."
It also called for an "immediate end to hostilities, renewed diplomatic action by all Member States for permanent peace, and third-state accountability through universal jurisdiction."

articles.title: Black Sea attacks push commercial ships into Marmara anchorages
articles.body:
(İHA Photo)
Hundreds of commercial vessels are crowding anchorages in the Marmara Sea as shipowners increasingly avoid the Black Sea amid a surge in attacks on civilian ships linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.
More than 200 commercial vessels bound for the Black Sea have been struck by unmanned aerial vehicles or missiles over the past four months, including Turkish-flagged ships.
The attacks have turned the Marmara Sea into a vast parking area, with hundreds of vessels dropping anchor rather than proceeding into the Black Sea.
Speaking to Turkish media, business representatives called for navigational safety to be restored in the Black Sea.
Yusuf Yalçın Çapoğlu, vice president of the Turkish Shipowners’ and Operators’ Association (KOSDER), said attacks brought commercial activity in the Black Sea to the brink of collapse.
“The number of vessels entering and leaving through the straits has fallen below 30. Under normal circumstances, that figure was above 200,” Çapoğlu said.
“Ukraine is doing everything it can to prevent vessels engaged in trade with Russia from going there. Russia is retaliating. Ships are being hit by missiles and drones. Recently, a vessel bound for Georgia was struck on its way there. The shipowner changed his mind and turned back. It was hit again on the way back,” he added.
Even when the vessels are not operating, shipowners continue to incur substantial costs for every day they remain at anchor.
“Whether you operate the vessel or not, you have to pay these expenses. They start at around $2,500 a day and can rise to $5,000, $6,000 or even $7,000,” Çapoğlu said.
He also warned that if there was no end in sight to the situation, shipowners could take the drastic step of unloading their vessels rather than continuing to operate under such conditions.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Sept. 15 said that to the growing number of attacks targeting civilian vessels in the Black Sea is unacceptable in remarks made in Azerbaijan.
Fidan said Türkiye had issued the necessary warnings to the parties, adding that he believed common ground could be found if the required political will was demonstrated and the two sides acted in good faith.

articles.title: Kyiv’s arms industry wants to kill the export fee. Parliament just refused to route that money to the army
articles.body:
Ukraine's arms industry wants the government to scrap a steep fee on weapons exports, warning it undercuts their prices just as Europe's defense market opens, RBC-Ukraine reported. The same fee has opened a second fight in Kyiv, where parliament this week declined to turn its revenue into money for the army.
Russia's war on Ukraine has pushed Europe into rearming, and Ukraine's battle-tested arms makers are among the few that can deliver at scale right now—an opening that domestic red tape could blunt, handing the advantage to competitors just as the market grows.
A €60 billion European window—and a fee in the way
The push comes as Europe opens a major market for Ukrainian weapons. The EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan for 2026-2027 reserves €60 billion for defense purchases, and partners increasingly want weapons built on their own soil. International partners report more than 200 cooperation approaches to Ukrainian firms still without a decision, according to the industry's press release. Producers link the fee fix to Build with Ukraine, a co-production push they consider strategically significant.
Ukraine’s Build with Ukraine has 200-plus foreign cooperation bids pending decision. Its arms industry, representing 400-plus firms, wants to help fix mechanism
Parliament won't route the money to the army
On 15 September, the Verkhovna Rada—Ukraine's parliament—rejected a bill in first reading that would have sent fee revenue collected from 1 August 2026 into a special budget fund for the Defense Ministry, half for buying, modernizing, and repairing weapons, half for soldiers' pay. The vote left the fee itself untouched, since it rests on the Cabinet resolution, and settled only that its revenue will not be earmarked for the army.
The fee producers want gone
The Ukrainian Council of Arms Manufacturers, joined by other defense and employer groups, prepared proposals to rework the July government resolution, No. 875. They want the fee—20% on finished goods and technologies, 30% on parts—cut to zero, or capped at 5%. Firms must also pay upfront, before any foreign payment lands, with no refund guaranteed if a deal collapses. A UAH 15 million (about $337,000) threshold shuts out the small test shipments new clients often begin with.
Ukraine put an Italian-Swiss Skyguard into combat duty. The missile inside is a Cold War design derived from the American Sparrow
The fee has drawn complaints since the resolution took effect in early July. Ihor Fedirko, the council's executive director, earlier said the 30-day review window was welcome but warned it could clog into a bureaucratic queue as staff leave the agencies running it. One of the associations behind the submission calls the 30% rate on parts prohibitive, since Europe is where Ukrainian firms would undercut Chinese suppliers on price.
Ukraine has swung from banning weapons sales abroad to courting foreign buyers, and its defense sector now ranks among the country's fastest-growing industries. Wartime certification to NATO standards is turning that output into something European militaries can actually buy.

articles.title: UK seeks allies for space-based missile warning network
articles.body:
Britain is working with NATO allies and other partners on future sensing capabilities for missile defence, including space-based systems intended to help detect, assess and track threats across the Euro-Atlantic.
The work was outlined in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made in finding partners for the next-generation persistent surveillance capability proposed in the 2025 Strategic Defence Review. The SDR called for an overhead intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capability able to sense, warn of and track threats across the Euro-Atlantic in support of Integrated Air and Missile Defence.
Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard said: “Defence is also improving the sensing capabilities that underpin Integrated Air and Missile Defence through a layered NATO-integrated approach, drawing on ground-based, airborne, maritime and space-based sensors to improve the ability to detect, assess and respond to threats across the Euro-Atlantic.”
Pollard said the money would initially be directed towards foundational elements of the system, including command and control, new radars and other sensing infrastructure.
He said: “For Integrated Air and Missile Defence (IAMD), the Defence Investment Plan invests a further £790 million in dedicated homeland IAMD, focused on improving foundational capabilities through enhanced Command and Control and sensing systems, including new radars and control systems.”
The Government is also investing in long-range weapons and Deep Precision Strike, including Precision Strike Missiles, as part of the wider effort to improve the ability of the Integrated Force to detect and respond to threats. The future sensing architecture is intended to work as part of NATO rather than as an isolated national system, bringing information from different domains into a common air and missile defence picture.
Pollard said Defence was “working closely with NATO as part of a layered and integrated approach to the defence of the UK and the Euro-Atlantic.”
On international participation, he said the National Armaments Director was already working with allies and partner nations to identify opportunities for joint development and procurement.

articles.title: Shares in Raiffeisen Bank International fell 9% after a short seller accused the lender of helping Russia evade sanctions. The bank called the report misleading and factually wrong.
articles.body:
Shares in Raiffeisen Bank International fell 9% after a short seller accused the lender of helping Russia evade sanctions. The bank called the report misleading and factually wrong.
Shares in Raiffeisen Bank International fell 9% during trading on September 17 after the short seller Grizzly Research published a report accusing the bank of helping Russia evade sanctions.
Raiffeisen said the report was misleading and contained factual errors. “We remain confident in the strength of our compliance systems, which have been audited repeatedly,” a bank spokesperson said. The spokesperson also said the company has spent years trying to sell its Russian business and leave Russia.
In its report, Grizzly Research called Raiffeisen and its Russian subsidiary “one of the key channels for evading sanctions.” The report’s authors say $1.19 billion in trade with Russia went through the bank, including trade in sanctioned goods used by Russia’s armed forces.
Analysts at Bloomberg Intelligence say Grizzly Research may be exaggerating Raiffeisen’s sanctions risks. In their view, transactions through the bank’s Russian subsidiary are not in themselves evidence of sanctions evasion.
The bigger risk comes from regulators: any close scrutiny from the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control or the European Central Bank could further complicate Raiffeisen’s already difficult exit from Russia.
Raiffeisen Bank International’s main asset in Russia is its subsidiary, AO Raiffeisenbank. AO Raiffeisenbank remains the largest Western lender in the country and has not been hit by Western sanctions.
Raiffeisen announced plans to wind down its Russian operations as early as the first weeks of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but it has yet to leave the Russian market.
Russian authorities are blocking the sale of Raiffeisen’s Russian business. Any deal requires their approval, but Moscow wants to keep the bank in Russia as a conduit for settling payments with Western countries, chiefly Europe. At the same time, the United States has pressured Raiffeisen over its dealings with Russia.

articles.title: Babcock reports strong demand across defence markets
articles.body:
Babcock has reported trading in line with expectations across the first five months of its financial year, with demand across its core defence markets remaining robust and full year guidance unchanged, the company stated in a trading update ahead of its annual general meeting.
The update records continued strong performance in nuclear and aviation, the completion of the chief executive transition, a further £200 million share buyback launched in July, and a £250 million six-year sterling bond extending the group’s debt maturity profile.
Harry Holt, who became group chief executive on 31 July, said: “Since becoming CEO, I have focused on maintaining disciplined execution, engagement with customers, shareholders and partners, investing in our people and sharpening the Group’s priorities for sustainable long-term growth.
“We have started FY27 with good momentum and operational delivery, supported by strong demand across our core defence and nuclear markets, while in the near term the UK Government continues to confirm the details of the implementation of their Defence Investment Plan.”
He said: “In this era of global tension and the rapidly changing nature of warfare, our priorities are clear: deliver for our customers, strengthen programme performance, maintain capital allocation discipline and convert our strong market positions into long-term growth.”
David Lockwood, his predecessor, remains with the group supporting the succession until his retirement in January 2027. According to the company, Holt has progressed a number of organisational and leadership changes aligned with his priorities, aimed at driving growth and accelerating transformation delivery.
On submarine support, the update records that a six-month bridging agreement on the Future Maritime Support Programme with the Ministry of Defence has allowed the company to continue delivering increasing levels of critical naval base and nuclear submarine fleet support while the longer-term Gateway support agreement is finalised.
Among the contracts secured, Babcock was awarded a CAD$1.2 billion six-year extension, worth around £600 million, to lead and deliver Victoria-class submarine in-service support for the Royal Canadian Navy, with the potential to extend to the fleet’s expected end of life in the late 2030s. It was also selected as preferred bidder for an eight-year contract supporting operational combat training for the French Air Force, which the company describes as its first combat flight training contract supporting France’s warfighting readiness.
A follow-on contract from the Ministry of Defence covers keeping Ukraine’s gifted military vehicles, including Challenger 2 tanks, frontline-operational. In Australia, a follow-on five-year contract worth around £60 million was awarded in partnership with Saab for through-life engineering and supply chain support to the Royal Australian Navy’s Anzac-class frigates.
The company has announced a collaboration with Supacat to enhance its General Logistics Vehicle offering for the British Army’s Light Mobility Vehicle programme, intended to replace the retiring Land Rover fleet, which it says builds on the delivery of the final British Army Jackal from its production line.
On exports, the update notes that Poland floated off its first Miecznik-class frigate, based on the Arrowhead 140 design, which the company describes as further evidence of the knowledge and technology transfer programme supporting Polish sovereign skills and industrial capability, and a key component of its frigate licence and export proposition.
Babcock welcomed the Defence Investment Plan published in June, noting the £298 billion of spend over four years with further clarity on funding expected at Budget 2026. It also referred to Project Royal Oak, the £26 billion programme announced at Devonport in August covering £7 billion for the naval base and dockyard and £15 billion to regenerate HM Naval Base Clyde, stating that as sole through-life support provider for the nuclear submarine fleet and incumbent site operator at both bases it is well placed to benefit.
On the hybrid navy, supported by around £1.5 billion over four years, the company says it is working with HII and Arondite through ARMOR Force to combine and develop autonomous systems, modular technology and digital innovation.
The group expects to publish its half year results on 19 November, at which Holt said he looks forward to sharing more.

articles.title: Zelenskyy reports shootdown of jet-powered drone by Ukrainian interceptor
articles.body:
During tests of a Ukrainian interceptor designed to counter jet-powered Shahed drones, one of these Russian UAVs was shot down, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced following a briefing by the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Mykhailo Drapaty.
“It’s important that there is another positive result from the tests of interceptors against jet-powered Shaheds: a downing. Thank you to all the developers and our warriors. We will scale it up,” Zelenskyy said on X Thursday.
The President also announced that Ukraine is preparing new active, long-range operations.
In addition, the head of state noted the necessary momentum in Donetsk region and reported on preparations to reinforce Kupyansk sector.
According to him, the Defense Forces are destroying the occupiers' positions in Oleksandrivka direction.

articles.title: Belarus Reactivates Relays Helping Russian Drones Strike Deeper Into Ukraine, Kyiv Says
articles.body:
Belarus has reactivated signal relays that help Russian attack drones penetrate deeper into Ukraine, including the western regions bordering Poland, Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service said.
The equipment amplifies signals for Russian Shahed and Gerbera drones, allowing them to fly farther into Ukrainian territory after entering from Russia, according to Border Guard spokesperson Andriy Demchenko.

“Belarus is actively assisting Russia” with attacks on Ukraine, Demchenko told Ukrinform on Sept. 16.
The relays allow Russian drones to stay close to the Belarusian border while receiving an amplified signal before moving deeper into Ukraine, including toward Rivne, Volyn and Lviv regions, he said.
Demchenko also linked the Belarusian support to a Russian drone attack on the Yahodyn border crossing with Poland on Sept. 13.
Russian drones struck a gas station near the crossing and a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw railway line. The Yahodyn crossing is about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border.
The latest claim comes after a series of Russian drone attacks reaching western Ukraine. Ukrainian officials have previously said Russian drones flying along the Belarusian border have used relay equipment on Belarusian territory to maintain their signals.
Belarus had turned the relays off
The equipment had previously been switched off after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Belarusian ruler Alexander Lukashenko in June to remove the relays from the border.
Russian Drone Hits Kharkiv Mall, Woman Needs Medical Aid
Zelensky said at the time that if Lukashenko did not remove the equipment, Ukraine would do it itself.
Several days later, Zelensky said the relays had stopped working as of June 22, although he said he did not know whether they had been physically dismantled.
Demchenko now says the equipment has been switched on again.
The Ukrainian Border Guard Service said there is currently no evidence of a Russian or Belarusian strike force building up near Ukraine’s border that would indicate preparations for a ground invasion.
But Kyiv continues to regard the Belarusian direction as a source of military support for Russia’s drone campaign.
